How Much Could AfCFTA Contribute to Economic Growth?
According to World Bank research, effective implementation of AfCFTA could increase Africa’s real income by approximately $450 billion by 2035 compared with a baseline without the agreement.

Which Industries Could Benefit?
Manufacturers could gain access to larger regional markets.
Logistics and transportation companies may benefit from increased cross-border goods movement.
Banks and payment providers could support additional trade financing, business payments, and corporate investment.
Agricultural businesses may also gain from improved regional supply chains and market access.

Implementation requires cooperation across national governments and regulatory bodies.
Border infrastructure, customs procedures, transportation networks, and non-tariff barriers remain important obstacles.

articles.title: Glencore cobalt output sinks 52% under DRC quotas - Mining.com
articles.summary: Glencore cobalt output sinks 52% under DRC quotas  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Glencore (LON: GLEN), one of the world’s largest cobalt producers, reported a 52% drop in output during the first nine months of 2026 as export quotas in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) prompted it to leave more of the battery metal unprocessed.
The Swiss-based miner produced 13,700 tonnes of its own-sourced cobalt through September, down from 28,500 tonnes a year earlier, according to its third-quarter production report released Thursday. Output fell 20% quarter-on-quarter to 3,500 tonnes.
Glencore said it is increasingly retaining cobalt contained in mixed ore in solution rather than converting it into saleable hydroxide, cutting near-term processing costs. The company expects to recover the metal’s value as export regulations evolve, but excludes the retained material from reported production.
The strategy illustrates how the DRC’s efforts to control cobalt supply are changing mining operations, with companies delaying processing rather than producing material they cannot immediately export. It also raises the prospect of additional supply entering the market once restrictions ease.
Cobalt restrictions
The DRC, the world’s dominant cobalt-producing country, suspended exports in 2025 after prices slumped to nine-year lows. Authorities subsequently introduced quotas aimed at supporting prices, with restrictions expected to remain in place until at least the end of 2027.
Glencore said its Kamoto Copper Company (KCC) and Mutanda operations hold enough cobalt stocks to meet near-term export allocations. Its African Copper division, which includes the Congolese mines, produced 11,600 tonnes of cobalt through September, down 56% year-on-year.
The volume of cobalt being held in solution remains undisclosed, making it difficult to assess how much additional supply could eventually reach the market.
Copper operations, meanwhile, delivered stronger results. Glencore’s own-sourced production rose 3% to 598,600 tonnes from 583,500 tonnes a year earlier. Excluding the closure of Mount Isa’s copper mine and the sale of Kidd, output increased 12% on a comparable basis.
Higher mining rates and improved grades at African Copper, together with richer ore at Peru’s Antamina mine, offset weaker production at Antapaccay and Collahuasi.
Glencore aims to produce 1.6 million tonnes of copper annually by 2035, nearly double its current level, as it pursues demand from electrification, power grids and artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Production outlook
The company maintained its 2026 copper guidance of 810,000 to 870,000 tonnes, although it expects to finish near the bottom of that range. Steelmaking coal output is also tracking toward the lower end of its 30 million to 32 million-tonne target, while zinc and energy coal are expected near the upper ends of their forecasts.
“We are pleased to report a strong third quarter production performance, where our key assets largely performed in line with expectations and previously communicated guidance,” CEO Gary Nagle said.
BMO Capital Markets analyst Alexander Pearce said in a note the company’s quarterly production was slightly below expectations overall. Copper and steelmaking coal missed estimates by 3% and 7%, respectively, while zinc and thermal coal exceeded forecasts by 4% and 5%.
Pearce noted Glencore’s full-year outlook remained broadly consistent with BMO’s forecasts, indicating that the quarterly shortfalls could be offset during the final three months of 2026.
Steelmaking coal production declined 13% to 21.5 million tonnes through September because of lower plant throughput and yields at its EVR operations. Energy coal output edged up to 73.9 million tonnes from 73.5 million tonnes a year earlier.
Glencore also advanced the restart of its ferrochrome smelters, bringing Boshoek back online in September and Wonderkop in October, following the earlier restart of Lion. Attributable ferrochrome production climbed 29% from the second quarter.
The company reiterated its forecast for full-year marketing, adjusted earnings before interest and taxes to exceed $5 billion.

articles.title: Nigeria’s API Production Can Boost Non-oil Exports, African Trade – FG - News Agency of Nigeria
articles.summary: Nigeria’s API Production Can Boost Non-oil Exports, African Trade – FG  News Agency of Nigeria
articles.full_text:
By Folasade Akpan
The Federal Government says Nigeria can become a regional supplier of pharmaceutical ingredients, deepen African pharmaceutical value chains and boost its non-oil exports if it develops the capacity to produce them competitively.
Dr Chris Isokpunwu, the Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment, said this on Friday in Abuja at the Future of Health Conference 2026, organised by Nigeria Health Watch in collaboration with the World Bank Group, in Abuja.
The meeting has “Accelerating the Shift to Domestic Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients Production for Priority Essential Medicines in Nigeria,” as theme.
Isokpunwu said Nigeria had the market, population and entrepreneurial capacity to develop a competitive pharmaceutical manufacturing industry.
He said that the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) also offered an opportunity to expand the market for locally manufactured pharmaceutical inputs.
“With the right production capacity and internationally competitive standards, Nigeria can position itself as a regional supplier of pharmaceutical inputs, deepen African value chains and strengthen its non-oil industrial exports,” he said.
He, however, said achieving this would require deliberate identification of priority essential medicines, assessment of the technical and commercial feasibility of local production and a phased approach to attracting credible investors.
He described domestic production of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) as a strategic imperative connecting public health, industrialisation, investment, trade and national security.
“Nigeria cannot achieve sustainable health security while remaining heavily dependent on external sources for critical pharmaceutical inputs,” he said.
According to him, local API production would strengthen medicine supply chains, reduce exposure to international disruptions and foreign exchange pressures, create skilled employment and retain more value within the Nigerian economy.
He identified predictable policies, an enabling regulatory environment, reliable power and other infrastructure, affordable financing and a sustainable market as essential conditions for attracting investment into local API manufacturing.
The permanent secretary said government also needed to support technology transfer, skills development, research and industrial partnerships, alongside effective coordination among relevant ministries and regulatory institutions.
He recalled that the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment had initiated the establishment of the Health Industries Corporation of Nigeria (HICON) to catalyse investment in APIs, basic medical hardware, pharmaceutical products, herbal medicines and diagnostic devices.
On his part, Dr Abdul Muktar, National Coordinator, Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC), said the initiative was working with the private sector to identify and prioritise APIs according to Nigeria’s public health needs.
Represented by Dr Zara Abba-Aji, he said PVAC was also collaborating with the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority (NSIA) on excipient manufacturing.
He noted that domestic pharmaceutical production required a holistic approach involving access to capital, workforce development and affordable medicines.
Muktar said the initiative was working with a local manufacturer to facilitate access to European Investment Bank (EIB) funding and technical expertise for manufacturing and technology transfer.
He described the federal government’s 2024 Executive Order, which provided local manufacturers access to precursor ingredients, including APIs, as a temporary measure towards achieving domestic production.
Also speaking, Dr Olumide Okunola of the World Bank Group and International Finance Corporation (IFC) said pharmaceutical manufacturing presented significant health and economic opportunities for Nigeria.
He said investments in the health economy could improve health outcomes, increase productivity, create jobs and strengthen national competitiveness.
Okunola cited a modelling report which estimated that developing Nigeria’s health economy could unlock more than 40 billion dollars in value, equivalent to nearly eight per cent of the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
He said Nigeria had about 200 pharmaceutical manufacturers, but their production capacity remained below 40 per cent due to challenges including regulation, inadequate power supply and financing constraints.
“Each and every single one of them needs to go to China, India to import their APIs even to make paracetamol,” he said.
Okunola said Nigeria could leverage its petrochemical infrastructure to develop domestic API production, while strategically identifying products that offered the greatest economic and health security value.
He also commended the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) for developing an API policy, describing it as an important first step towards establishing a foundation for domestic production.
In her remarks, the Managing Director, Nigeria Health Watch, Vivianne Ihekweazu, said Nigeria’s dependence on imported pharmaceutical ingredients exposed its medicine supply chain to foreign exchange fluctuations and international disruptions.
She said the COVID-19 pandemic had demonstrated the vulnerability of countries that depended on external sources for essential medicines and other health supplies.
Ihekweazu said the conference was focusing on how Nigeria could strengthen its capacity to manufacture the ingredients required for essential medicines, adding that medicine security was an important component of health system resilience.
She said access to affordable medicines remained a major concern, noting that local production could help address cost pressures associated with imported ingredients.
She called for coordinated action by the ministries of health and industry, regulators, financial institutions and the private sector to create an enabling environment for sustainable pharmaceutical manufacturing.
Similarly, the Chief Executive Officer, Bloom Public Health, Prof. Chimezie Anyakora, said Nigeria had reached a stage where it should move beyond manufacturing finished pharmaceutical products to producing its active ingredients.
He said the country had developed considerable capacity in medicine manufacturing and should now advance further along the pharmaceutical value chain.
“Nigeria is among the biggest consumption and manufacturing countries in Africa. We need to be among those that will move to API manufacturing,” he said.
Anyakora said the transition would require specialised skills and urged universities to prepare professionals for the emerging area of pharmaceutical production.
He commended local manufacturers investing in API production, saying more companies needed to embrace the process.
He also called for greater public participation in ensuring medicine quality, noting that the responsibility of combating fake and substandard medicines should not rest solely with NAFDAC.
He said Nigerian pharmaceutical manufacturing had improved considerably over the past decade, adding that sustained investment in technical capacity and regulatory oversight would further strengthen confidence in locally manufactured medicines.
The (NAN) reports that the Future of Health Conference which began on Thursday, provides a platform for stakeholders to examine how health innovations, partnerships, research and sustainable financing can improve healthcare delivery in Nigeria.
The 2026 edition, themed “From Innovation to Impact: The Future of Health is Now”, focuses on practical solutions, scaling effective interventions and strengthening health systems to achieve measurable health outcomes.(NAN)

articles.title: Ramaphosa Hints At AGOA Exclusion, Experts Discuss Potential Implications For South Africa - Forbes Africa
articles.summary: Ramaphosa Hints At AGOA Exclusion, Experts Discuss Potential Implications For South Africa  Forbes Africa
articles.full_text:
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) continues to be a key economic factor in South Africa as the country considers the potential implications, should it not be renewed.
During a briefing with editors and reporters on October 19, South Africa’s President Cyril Ramaphosa opened up about a possible AGOA exclusion, saying, “I need, as president, to prepare us if it ever happens”.
So, what could an exit mean for South Africa?
For a country stressed by a high unemployment rate, sitting at over 30%, job losses will surely be one of Ramaphosa’s primary concerns.
“The most immediate consequences would be felt by export-oriented industries that have historically benefitted from AGOA, including agriculture and manufacturing…. Reduced competitiveness in the U.S. market could translate into lower export volumes, pressure on profitability and, ultimately, job losses,” says Lisette IJssel de Schepper, Chief Economist at the University of Stellenbosch-based Bureau for Economic Research (BER), to FORBES AFRICA.
Loading...
This would come as diplomatic tensions between the U.S. and South Africa have failed to dissipate.
In May last year, Ramaphosa visited Washington to resolve President Donald Trump’s unproven genocide claims. Multilateral relations later took another knock when Trump declined his invitation to the 2025 G20 summit in Johannesburg in November, effectively tarnishing the traditional handover ceremony between the two nations.
This year will see Trump chair the G20 in Miami, and he has made claims about barring South Africa from the event.
AGOA, which South Africa has benefited from since its inception in 2000 under U.S. President Bill Clinton, has been another delicate matter and was temporarily expired until a one-year deal was introduced in February this year.
Later extended to December 2028, the U.S. Congress voted for South Africa to remain, but it’s Trump who has the final say.
“We are not the first and only country to be taken out of AGOA. And I believe we will not be the last,” Ramaphosa said in the briefing regarding the hypothetical instance of an expulsion, admitting that such an outcome would be “devastating” for the economy.
Given the “broader deterioration” of South Africa-U.S. trade relations, IJssel de Schepper makes an notable point as to how fruitful AGOA has been of late.
“The tariffs introduced over the past year have eroded many of the benefits associated with AGOA, so some of the economic consequences are already being felt.”
Though there is no question that more pain would be felt for South Africa’s economy.
Jee-A van der Linde, Oxford Economics Africa’s Senior Economist, believes the possible fallout would “further erode South Africa’s manufacturing base,” since the nature of the goods sent to the U.S. are heavy and developed, including everything from cars to wine.
Asked if he sees any positives from switching focus to alternative markets, van der Linde says he doesn’t currently see them.
He points out that while South Africa welcomed China’s zero-tariff scheme in June last year, the Asian powerhouse mostly orders raw materials.
And as for Africa, van der Linde believes that offers slim expansion: “I don’t think there’s sufficient regional demand for pricier goods compared to the likes of China.”
With GDP growth plateauing at around 1% over the past few years, South Africa is already tasked with trying to accelerate its trajectory; an AGOA omission would surely increase the gradient of this battle.

articles.title: EU Extends GSP to 2036, Keeping Duty-Free Access for Tanzanian Exports - TanzaniaInvest
articles.summary: EU Extends GSP to 2036, Keeping Duty-Free Access for Tanzanian Exports  TanzaniaInvest
articles.full_text:
On 26th October 2026, the European Union (EU) confirmed a 10-year extension of its Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) during an EU–Africa trade press briefing.
The announcement comes as the EU marks 25 years of the Everything But Arms (EBA) scheme and 25 years of formal EU–Africa political relations, which began with the 2000 Cairo Summit.
The extension of the GSP framework means that the EU will be maintaining predictable trade arrangements for developing countries including Tanzania and confirming that the EBA scheme will continue indefinitely for eligible least developed countries (LDCs).
Under the EBA scheme, eligible LDCs will continue to receive automatic, duty-free and quota-free access to the EU market for all products except arms and ammunition, without an expiry date or the need to reapply for the arrangement.
The revised GSP framework will take effect on 1st January 2027 and run for 10 years, through 2036.
Beyond tariff preferences, EU–Africa trade cooperation is increasingly focused on expanding local processing, supporting regional value addition, and strengthening sustainable supply chains.
According to the EU, the Union remains Africa’s largest trade and investment partner as trade in goods between the two partners increased by 51%, from EUR 236 billion in 2016 to EUR 357 billion in 2025. The EU accounts for 33% of Africa’s total trade in goods and is the destination for almost 40% of African exports over the past 25 years.
In 2024, EU companies held more than EUR 250 billion in foreign direct investment stock in Africa, while African investments in the EU exceeded EUR 74 billion and African exports under EBA to the EU increased from EUR 112 million to nearly EUR 5 billion in 2025.
At a national level, Tanzania recorded a 96% utilisation rate for available trade preferences under the scheme, indicating that its exporters are making substantial use of the market access available to eligible products.
Continued EBA access provides an established route for Tanzania into the EU market, the extent to which the country benefits will depend in part on exporters’ ability to use available preferences, meet EU product standards and expand the value of goods produced for export.
Speaking on the matter, the European Commission Spokesperson for Trade, Economic Security and Customs, Olof Gill, stated: “The EU-Africa relationship is a true partnership of equals. Our trade and investment approach is designed to deliver maximum mutual benefit: supporting Africa’s ambitions for sustainable development, industrialisation and jobs, while at the same time helping Europe diversify its partnerships and build resilient supply chains.”
Gill reiterated: “In an increasingly unpredictable geopolitical context, the EU remains Africa’s first trade and investment partner, with longstanding agreements rooted in stability, predictability, and sustainability. 33% of Africa’s total trade in goods is with the EU, which is also the first destination of Africa’s exports, accounting for almost 40%. Both sides benefit from strong trade relations and cooperation. Africa ranks as the EU’s fourth-largest trade partner. Over the past decade, EU trade with Africa has grown by 51%, from EUR 236 billion in 2016 to EUR 357 billion in 2025. Overall, 44 African countries have duty-free access to the EU market, a market of 450 million consumers, and 97% of African exports enter the EU free of import duties.”
“At the same time, compliance with high EU standards opens up other potential markets and makes African products more competitive elsewhere. European investors hold the largest foreign direct investment stock in Africa. In 2024, the investments of EU companies in Africa were worth over EUR 250 billion, while African investments in the EU were worth over EUR 74 billion,” added Gill.
Gill confirmed: “With the 6 Economic Partnership Agreements with 15 countries currently in place, EU’s total trade with African EPA countries increased by 35%, and its foreign direct investment stock in African EPA countries increased from EUR 72 billion in 2014 to EUR 86 billion in 2024. This clearly shows that our Economic Partnership Agreements work and bring tangible benefits to economies on both sides.”
“These Economic Partnership Agreements with six countries in the Southern African Development Community (SADC), Cote d’Ivoire and Ghana were signed 10 years ago and since then our bilateral trade has increased, driving higher value added in the partner countries such as the automotive sector in South Africa or the cocoa sector in West Africa, attracting more investment imports by 61% since 2015,” noted Gill.
The EU’s Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) is a unilateral trade preference scheme that reduces or removes customs duties on eligible goods imported to the EU from developing countries.
It was established in 1971, following international efforts through the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) to help developing countries participate more fully in global trade and it’s current framework entered into force in January 2014.
The EU’s GSP comprises three arrangements: 1) Standard GSP, which provides for the partial or full removal of customs duties on two-thirds of tariff lines for eligible developing countries; 2) GSP+, which offers zero tariffs on these products to eligible vulnerable countries that meet additional requirements; 3) the Everything But Arms (EBA) arrangement, which grants least developed countries duty-free, quota-free access to the EU market for all products except arms and ammunition.

articles.title: [不同来源] FROM REFORMS TO DELIVERY: OUR INFRASTRUCTURE INVESTMENT AND GROWTH STRATEGY - News Agency of Nigeria
articles.summary: FROM REFORMS TO DELIVERY: OUR INFRASTRUCTURE INVESTMENT AND GROWTH STRATEGY  News Agency of Nigeria
articles.full_text:
By President Bola Ahmed Tinubu
Since 2023, we have made difficult but necessary decisions: removing the petrol subsidy, unifying the exchange rate, modernising the tax framework, and coordinating action on inflation. These reforms have restored macro balance, quadrupled federation revenue since 2021 and rebuilt the credibility of the State’s balance sheet. The results are now visible: real GDP growth reached 4.43% in Q2 2026 and 4.2% in H1, up from 2.74% in 2023, while headline inflation fell to 14.63% in September 2026 from 20.98% a year earlier.
Food inflation, while still elevated, stood at 19.59%. Gross external reserves reached USD 55.1 billion as of 9 October 2026, including about USD 46 billion in net reserves, an 18-year high. The NFEM exchange rate stood at ₦1,333/US$, with the market spread below 5%, and public debt remains low compared to peers. Nigeria’s cost of borrowing keeps falling. Confidence has a price, our cost of borrowing is going down, and the country risk premium has drastically decreased.
This changes the purpose of public borrowing. The objective is to increasingly direct new borrowing towards productive capital investment, while maintaining fiscal discipline, reducing refinancing pressures and ensuring that public debt translates into measurable value. Nigeria borrows to invest in roads, ports, rail and power that will generate growth, revenue and jobs for decades.
Every Naira and every dollar raised goes to assets that create value, and that value repays the debt. This is how Nigeria will reach the objective of a USD 1 trillion economy by 2030: not through consumption, but through investment in the infrastructure that makes growth possible. This shift is being supported by a stronger fiscal position: tax-to-GDP has risen to 12.5% from 7%, net FAAC increased by 44% from ₦15.2 trillion in 2024 to ₦21.9 trillion in 2025, and Nigeria recorded a ₦20.1 trillion trade surplus in H1 2026, almost double the ₦10.2 trillion recorded in H1 2025.
Borrowing to build, not to bridge, not for consumption:
Nigeria is fundamentally changing the purpose of public borrowing: from financing short-term fiscal pressures to investing in assets that will transform the economy for generations. This shift is taking place with public debt at 35.75% of GDP in Q2 2026 and debt service at about 65% of revenue in H1 2026, underscoring why investment must remain anchored in fiscal discipline.
The Federal Executive Council economic strategy is clear on this point: no deficit monetisation and no unfunded commitments during the pre-election period. At the heart of this disciplined shift towards productive borrowing are our administration’s legacy projects:
The administration is focusing productive borrowing on financing major infrastructure projects, including the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway; improvements to the power sector and electricity grid; the Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway; the Trans-Sahara Superhighway; and upgrades to Nigeria’s major commercial ports in Lagos.
Together with other priority projects, the rehabilitation of key hospitals, and investment in education and vocational training, these investments are game-changing. They will connect entire economic regions, unlock agricultural and industrial potential, reduce logistics costs, attract private investment and create hundreds of thousands of direct and indirect employment opportunities over time.
Delivery is already visible on the Lagos-Calabar highway as a major transport infrastructure project as of August 2026. Lot 2 was reported to be over 80% complete, while Calabar–Akwa Ibom works were over 30% complete. This increased emphasis on investment is also evident at the subnational level, where the share of state spending devoted to capital expenditure rose from 46% in 2023 to 61% in 2025.
This is not simply about building infrastructure. It is about reshaping Nigeria’s economic geography, unlocking new sources of growth and creating the productive capacity to achieve a USD 1 trillion economy. The debt is finite; the economic value these assets can generate will endure for generations.
II. Value for money and impact on growth:
The legacy projects are selected and financed on value addition: what they return to the economy for every Naira spent. They connect production to markets, ports to the hinterland and Nigeria to its neighbours. The Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway alone is expected to reduce logistics costs by 15–20% along the corridor and could add up to 2% to Nigeria’s GDP through new industrial zones, trade and tourism.
These projects are also among the largest job creators in the country. The Coastal Highway is expected to generate around 100,000 direct jobs in construction and engineering and more than 150,000 indirect jobs in logistics, materials and services.
Across the Sokoto–Badagry and Trans-Sahara corridors, the same logic applies to the enhancement of the power grid, ports, rail lines, and social infrastructure: jobs during construction, and lasting employment in the industries, farms, and businesses that grow along the routes once they open.
Lower transport costs mean lower food prices, more competitive exports and stronger revenue for the State. That is value for money: assets that pay back through growth, jobs and revenue, financed over a horizon that matches their life, and each one a step towards the USD 1 trillion economy.
III Long-term commitments for long-term assets:
The structure of Nigeria’s debt now matches the nature of what it finances. The government is extending the maturity profile and shifting from short-term borrowing to long- and very long-term maturities at lower cost. Infrastructure built to last forty years should be financed over a horizon consistent with its life. International investors are willing to commit to Nigeria over ten, fifteen years and beyond, which is the clearest signal of confidence in the country’s trajectory. The broader financing environment is also benefiting from monetary easing: the Monetary Policy Rate was cut by 350 basis points on 22 September 2026, from 26.5% to 23%.
Yet lending rates remain above 30%, reinforcing the need to secure longer-tenor, more competitive financing for productive investment.
IV. Credibility recognised by international markets:
The international financial community has delivered a clear and unprecedented convergence of positive signals on Nigeria. All three major credit rating agencies (S&P, Fitch and Moody’s) have taken positive rating actions, with S&P upgrading Nigeria’s sovereign rating and Fitch and Moody’s raising their outlooks to Positive.
FTSE Russell has restored Nigeria to Frontier Market status, reopening its visibility to global institutional investors, while the FATF has removed Nigeria from its grey list, recognising progress in financial transparency and compliance. Nigeria’s successful Eurobond issuance, attracting strong international demand, further demonstrates renewed investor appetite for Nigerian sovereign risk. The specific rating actions reinforce this convergence: Fitch rates Nigeria B with a Positive outlook as of 9 October 2026; Moody’s rates it B3 with a Positive outlook; and S&P upgraded Nigeria to B on 15 May 2026 with a Stable outlook.
Nigeria’s exit from the FATF Grey List in October 2025 and the EU list in January 2026 further supports improved financial transparency and compliance. These are not endorsements; they are independent assessments by global rating agencies, index providers, regulators and investors, recognising stronger external reserves, improved macroeconomic management and greater financial credibility. The implications are transformative: broader access to international capital, greater investor participation, and the potential for lower financing costs and longer maturities. Every improvement in Nigeria’s cost of capital creates additional capacity to finance infrastructure, accelerate growth and deliver my government’s transformation agenda.
V. What the international community expects:
The message from international investors, global banks and development institutions is unequivocal: Nigeria has undertaken the reforms; now is the time to invest, build and deliver at scale. International capital increasingly sees Nigeria as a major infrastructure investment opportunity, with lenders showing a growing appetite to finance our growth projects (Roads, Railways, Electricity, Water and Agriculture, Transport, and Social Infrastructure) and support the country’s long-term development.
Improving market confidence is creating opportunities for more competitive financing terms and greater access to long-term capital.
Nigeria must seize this window of opportunity. The greatest risk is no longer simply the cost of borrowing, but the economic cost of failing to invest. This changes the purpose of public borrowing. The objective is to increasingly direct new borrowing towards productive capital investment, while maintaining fiscal discipline, reducing refinancing pressures and ensuring that public debt translates into measurable economic value. Nigeria borrows to invest in roads, ports, rail and power that will generate growth, revenue and jobs for decades.

articles.full_text:
- Rio Tinto inaugurated two new lithium plants worth $1.4 billion in Argentina, boosting annual production capacity by 25,000 metric tonnes.
- The investments strengthen Rio Tinto's position in the growing global lithium market, essential for electric vehicles and batteries.
- Rio Tinto's global investment strategy also includes a $6.2 billion commitment to Guinea's Simandou iron ore project and a $473 million restart of mineral sands in South Africa.
- Together, these initiatives expand Rio Tinto's presence across key commodity markets, including lithium, iron ore, and mineral sands in Argentina, Guinea, South Africa, and Madagascar.
The Anglo-Australian group officially opened the Sal de Vida plant and Fénix 1B expansion in Argentina's Catamarca province on October 28, 2026, adding a combined 25,000 metric tonnes of annual lithium carbonate equivalent production capacity.
According to Reuters, the investment strengthens Rio Tinto's position in the global lithium market as demand increases for minerals used in electric vehicles and battery storage systems.
The company ranked fourth among publicly listed mining groups by market capitalisation in October 2026, with an estimated valuation of $139.4 billion.
Rio Tinto expands lithium production in Argentina
Sal de Vida is expected to produce 15,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent annually, while the Fénix 1B expansion will contribute another 10,000 tonnes once both facilities reach full capacity.
Rio Tinto is also developing its Rincón project in Argentina's Salta province, targeting annual production capacity of 60,000 tonnes as part of its broader ambition to reach 200,000 tonnes of global lithium capacity by 2028.
Speaking at the inauguration, chief executive Simon Trott outlined the company's production ambitions.
"We live in an era in which the world needs more lithium. At Rio Tinto, we have set ourselves the goal of reaching 200,000 tons of annual production capacity, with opportunities to raise that figure much higher," Trott said.
The expansion relies partly on direct lithium extraction technology, which can shorten processing times compared with conventional evaporation methods, although questions remain about operating costs and commercial scalability.
Rio Tinto's investments extend across Africa
Beyond Argentina, Rio Tinto is advancing its estimated $6.2 billion funding commitment to Guinea's Simandou iron ore project, one of Africa's largest mining and infrastructure developments.
The investment forms part of an $11.6 billion programme covering the SimFer mine and associated railway and port infrastructure.
Simandou is designed to support annual exports of up to 120 million tonnes of iron ore at full capacity, with Rio Tinto's SimFer joint venture responsible for blocks three and four, targeting 60 million tonnes.
The development recorded its first iron ore shipment in December 2025, with further construction continuing in 2026.
Meanwhile, Rio Tinto approved a $473 million investment in March 2026 to restart the Zulti South mineral sands project at Richards Bay Minerals in South Africa.
The project, suspended since 2020, is expected to extend operations until 2050, with initial commercial production scheduled for late 2028.
Beyond Guinea and South Africa, the mining group also maintains mineral sands operations in Madagascar through QIT Madagascar Minerals, which produces ilmenite for international industrial markets.
The investments span different commodity markets, with Rio Tinto's Argentine operations focused on lithium for battery manufacturing, while its African projects supply iron ore and minerals used in construction, manufacturing and other industries.

Ethiopia is seeking Chinese investment in strategic minerals and digital infrastructure as it moves to expand economic cooperation with Beijing in sectors gaining importance amid global competition over critical mineral supplies and technology development.
Deputy Commissioner of the Ethiopian Investment Commission (EIC) Meleket Sahlu and Chinese Embassy Economic Counselor Liu Xiaoguang held discussions on attracting investors to potash and rare earth projects, expanding bilateral trade and supporting the implementation of Ethiopia's Digital Ethiopia 2030 strategy, according to the commission.
The talks come as China, Ethiopia's largest trading partner and leading source of foreign investment, strengthens economic cooperation with African countries in mining, manufacturing and digital infrastructure. China also holds a dominant position in global rare earth processing, a sector receiving increased attention from major economies seeking to secure supplies of minerals used in electric vehicles, renewable energy technologies and electronics.
Bilateral trade between Ethiopia and China reached a record 4.72 billion US dollars in 2025, an increase of 32.8 percent from the previous year, according to Chinese foreign ministry data.
The two countries elevated their diplomatic relations to an All-Weather Strategic Partnership in October 2023. Ethiopia's admission to BRICS in January 2024 also brought the country into the grouping of emerging economies that includes China.
During the meeting, Meleket called for joint efforts to identify Chinese investors interested in developing Ethiopia's potash and rare earth mineral resources.
Ethiopia holds substantial potash deposits in the Danakil Depression, while exploration has identified potential rare earth mineral resources. Potash is widely used in fertilizer production, while rare earth elements are important inputs in clean energy technologies, electronics and advanced manufacturing.
China dominates global rare earth processing and permanent magnet production. The United States, European Union and Japan have been pursuing measures to diversify critical mineral supply chains, including through investment and trade partnerships with mineral-producing countries.
Several African countries have sought to attract foreign capital into mineral exploration, extraction and processing as international demand for critical minerals increases.
Ethiopia has designated mining as a priority sector under its ten-year development plan, with the government seeking to increase mineral exports and attract investment in gold, potash and industrial minerals.
Development of potash projects in the Danakil region has faced financing and infrastructure constraints, including the cost of transporting output from remote mining areas to export ports. Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti for access to international maritime trade.
The commission did not disclose the names of potential Chinese investors or announce financing commitments for specific mining projects.
The officials also discussed implementation of agreements signed between Ethiopian exporters and Chinese buyers under the "Export to China" initiative, which is intended to increase Ethiopian exports and address the imbalance in bilateral trade.
Ethiopia has traditionally exported agricultural commodities, including coffee, sesame and soybeans, to China, while importing machinery, electrical equipment, vehicles and other manufactured products.
The agreements cover agricultural and other export products and are intended to expand access to the Chinese market.
Ethiopian authorities have also been negotiating with Chinese counterparts over food safety requirements, product certification and customs procedures to facilitate the entry of additional export products.
China has expanded preferential market access for African products, although exporters remain subject to applicable sanitary, quality and customs requirements.
The discussions on trade come as Ethiopia seeks to diversify its export earnings and improve foreign exchange availability under ongoing economic reforms.
Digital development formed another part of the meeting, with the two sides discussing ways to promote Chinese investment in projects associated with Digital Ethiopia 2030.
Ethiopia launched the strategy in December 2025, outlining plans to expand mobile and internet connectivity, accelerate the rollout of fifth-generation telecommunications services and develop artificial intelligence, digital payments and electronic government systems.
The strategy builds on Digital Ethiopia 2025, under which mobile subscriptions reached approximately 97 million and internet users 57 million, according to government figures.
The 2030 strategy also targets expansion of data centre capacity, cloud infrastructure, digital skills and cybersecurity capabilities.
Chinese telecommunications companies Huawei and ZTE have maintained a longstanding presence in Ethiopia, supplying equipment and participating in network expansion projects involving state-owned Ethio Telecom.
Ethiopia began liberalising its telecommunications sector in 2021 with the licensing of Safaricom Ethiopia, introducing competition into a market previously dominated by Ethio Telecom.
Digital infrastructure has become an important area of international economic competition, with Chinese companies expanding their presence in telecommunications networks, cloud services and related technologies across Africa.
Ethiopia's Digital Ethiopia 2030 strategy includes provisions for digital sovereignty and data governance alongside efforts to attract investment and expand access to technology services.
Chinese involvement in Ethiopia's economy has extended beyond telecommunications to manufacturing, industrial parks and major infrastructure projects.
Chinese companies have participated in the development of the Eastern Industrial Zone and other industrial facilities, as well as the construction of the Addis Ababa–Djibouti railway, a principal transport link connecting landlocked Ethiopia with international maritime trade routes.
The railway, financed largely through Chinese loans and built by Chinese contractors, is among the major infrastructure projects associated with cooperation under China's Belt and Road Initiative.
The latest discussions follow the expansion of bilateral cooperation under the strategic partnership established in 2023, which covers trade, investment, infrastructure, industrial development and emerging technologies.
During the meeting, Liu described China as a key economic and investment partner and said expanded cooperation in trade, industry, mining and digital development would benefit both countries.
Meleket cited the longstanding relationship between Ethiopia and China and called for stronger investment cooperation, particularly in identifying companies capable of undertaking large-scale projects.
She said the commission is implementing a targeted investment promotion strategy and emphasised the importance of coordination with the Chinese Embassy to identify suitable investors.
The commission said the discussions would support efforts to promote Ethiopia's investment opportunities, attract strategic investors and strengthen long-term economic cooperation between the two countries.
No new investment commitments or project implementation timelines were announced following the talks.

He explained that the agreement provides for extensive trade liberalisation, covering approximately 99% of the total value of existing bilateral trade and 97% of all tariff lines.

Al Zeyoudi emphasised that the agreement places significant importance on services and investment, pointing to the scale of UAE investments in Canada. He recalled the announcement of US$50 billion in planned UAE investments in Canada during the Canadian Prime Minister's visit to the UAE last year.

Webuild has been selected as the preferred bidder for Lot 1B of the Lobito Corridor Railway Project in Zambia. This major infrastructure development is among the strategic initiatives supported by the Italian Government’s Mattei Plan for Africa. The entire project is set to transform commercial and trade connections across Southern Africa with global markets: once completed, it will reduce transit times for goods from the Copperbelt to international markets from 16 to 7 days, unlocking estimated economic benefits of approximately USD 3 billion for Zambia and Angola. The project will also offer an opportunity for Italy’s supply chain in the construction industry, helping develop one of the major strategic infrastructures in Africa.
The project is developed and sponsored by Africa Finance Corporation (AFC), the multilateral African financial institution, which has worked closely with the governments of Angola and Zambia to coordinate key approvals, align priorities and advance the project towards implementation. The project is supported by international development partners. The lot includes the engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) of a section of the railway running from the Angolan border to Chingola, in the heart of the Copperbelt province in Zambia.
The alignment traverses regions lacking large-scale infrastructure, and features 22 bridges and viaducts, 8 stations, and 3 maintenance depots designed to support heavy freight traffic volumes. Joining Webuild in the international consortium are Turkish contractor İçtaş (30%) and Portuguese contractor Mota-Engil (30%). It will connect Angola’s Atlantic port of Lobito to the key mining districts of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, home to vast resources of copper, cobalt, and other strategic minerals vital for the energy transition.
It is for this reason that the corridor is designated a priority for Italy within the Mattei Plan, as well as for the United States, the European Union, and G7 countries, which have included it among the flagship initiatives of the Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment (PGII) and the European Global Gateway, serving as critical infrastructure to diversify and secure supply chains for critical minerals.
Lot 1B represents the Zambian section of the broader Zambia Lobito Railway Project, which encompasses approximately 831 kilometres of greenfield railway between Zambia and Angola. articles.full_text:
Uncertainty has become the new normal for global businesses, with a mix of geopolitical tensions and macroeconomic concerns forcing them to prioritise resilience and restructure supply chains. This has impacted global Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), which fell by 11 per cent in 2024, following a 10 per cent drop in 2023, according to the ASEAN Investment Report 2025.
Against this backdrop, Southeast Asia has defied the odds and emerged as the bright spot for growth, with foreign direct investment (FDI) growing year on year. In 2024, Southeast Asia accounted for 15 per cent of global FDI inflows, attracting US$226 billion, a rise of 8 per cent from 2023. Since 2021, annual FDI inflows have consistently exceeded US$200 billion, above the previous decade’s annual average of under US$130 billion.
In fact, FDI stock in ASEAN rose from US$1 trillion in 2010 to US$3.6 trillion in 2024, equivalent to 1.2 times the combined stock in Africa and South America. Here are five highlights from the report that explain why MNCs are doubling down on Southeast Asia and why Singapore is their strategic hub for expansion.
1. More greenfield investments across diverse manufacturing sectors
Investments into Southeast Asia are increasingly driven by new and expansionary projects. More than two-thirds of inflows comprise of equity capital, while cross-border mergers and acquisitions fell by 61 per cent from 2023.
This signals that businesses are not simply acquiring firms or restructuring their balance sheets. Instead, they are establishing new operations, expanding production capacity, and building long-term capabilities across the region.
Furthermore, manufacturing FDI rose sharply, increasing by 147 per cent year-on-year, particularly in supply chain-intensive sectors such as automotive, electronics and semiconductors. Many of these big-ticket investments were either first-time entries into Southeast Asia or involved significant upgrading and expansion of existing facilities. These investments were driven by rising regional demand and the adoption of advanced manufacturing technologies to improve efficiency and resilience.
Investment spanned major economies, with Chinese firms active in automotive and apparel, US firms in pharmaceuticals and semiconductors, UK investors in aerospace and energy, and other Asian multinationals across automotive and electronics.
2. Digital economy investment is accelerating
Alongside manufacturing growth, investment in Southeast Asia’s digital economy is rising rapidly. Greenfield investment in digital-related sectors more than doubled to US$16 billion in 2024, reflecting rising demand and growing investor confidence in the region’s digital infrastructure, connectivity, and technology ecosystem.
This growth was driven by expansion in data centres, cloud services, software development and technology-enabled business activities. These investments are critical as they strengthen the region’s digital backbone – supporting advanced manufacturing, supply chain coordination, digital trade and cross-border services.
Some of these investments in Singapore include Amazon’s AWS APAC Hub, OpenAI’s APAC Hub, and Databrick’s Asia Pacific & Japan Hub.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a key digital technology across Southeast Asia, with companies adopting AI to enhance their supply chains by optimising logistics and improving inventory management. Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand are leading the region in industrial robot installations, with Singapore ranking second globally in robot density, with 730 robots per 10,000 employees in 2023 – significantly above the global average of 162.

Ethiopia Emerges as Leading Healthcare Manufacturing Hub in Africa: Expert
Addis Ababa, October 29, 2026 (ENA)— Ethiopia is becoming a premier destination for healthcare manufacturing investment in Africa, driven by bold policy reforms, improved foreign exchange access, and an open investment environment, according to Dr. Iain Barton, Founding Principal of Health 4 Development.
Speaking to ENA on the sidelines of the African Healthcare Manufacturing Trade Exhibition and Conference (AHMTEC 2026) in Addis Ababa, Dr. Barton noted that recent reforms have significantly transformed the nation's business climate.
He emphasized that these changes are creating major new opportunities for investors across the pharmaceutical and broader healthcare manufacturing sectors.
                
Barton, who has worked in Ethiopia’s pharmaceutical sector for nearly two decades, recalled that the country had previously been a difficult market to serve because of import restrictions and foreign exchange constraints. However, he said the situation had changed considerably over the past three years.
“What we’ve seen over the last 36 months is a complete transformation of the Ethiopian market,” he said. “I’ve always called Ethiopia the jewel of the East. It is such an incredible economy and such an incredible population. And suddenly it’s opened up.”
He attributed the transformation to government led reforms in regulation, foreign exchange management, investment incentives, and business ownership, saying the changes were helping attract renewed investor interest.
“Those policies are what is driving this transformation,” Barton said, adding that the impact could extend beyond healthcare manufacturing to other sectors of the economy.
He said Ethiopia’s large population and economic potential made it an increasingly important market for companies seeking to expand their presence across Africa.
While countries such as Nigeria, Tanzania, Rwanda, Egypt, Morocco, and Algeria also offer significant investment opportunities, Barton said Ethiopia should be central to companies’ long-term strategies for the continent.
“Anyone who doesn’t have Ethiopia on their strategic plan is missing the biggest opportunity of the moment,” he said.
Barton also highlighted Ethiopia’s potential within Africa’s broader drive to expand local production of medicines, vaccines, and medical devices, a move aimed at strengthening the continent’s capacity to meet its healthcare needs.
Referring to Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director General Dr. Jean Kaseya’s description of African manufacturing as “the second liberation of Africa,” Barton stressed the importance of developing domestic production capacity and making better use of the continent’s human and economic resources.
                
“We have to allow ourselves to explore our talents, explore our capacity, explore our market potential, and deliver against the promise we have made to the patients we serve,” he said. “If we do that effectively, our dreams know no bounds.”
He also commended African entrepreneurs for building businesses and creating economic value despite challenging operating conditions.
To sustain this progress, he called on governments to strengthen investment in universities, research and development, innovation hubs, and other support systems needed to nurture local talent and industrial capacity.
“All we have to do is give our talent the space, the opportunity, and the capacity,” he said.
AHMTEC 2026, held in Addis Ababa from October 26 to 28 under the theme “Industrialize to Commercialize,” brought together manufacturers, policymakers, investors, regulators, and development partners to explore ways to strengthen Africa’s healthcare manufacturing ecosystem and expand the continent’s capacity to produce essential health products locally.

Ethiopia has announced plans to establish itself as a leading pharmaceutical manufacturing centre in Africa, with a strategy focused on expanding local medicine production, strengthening regional supply chains and reducing dependence on imported healthcare products.
The initiative is part of the country’s wider ambition to improve healthcare security, attract investment and increase the availability of essential medicines, vaccines and medical equipment across the continent.
Ethiopia’s State Minister for Health, Muluken Argaw, outlined the plans on Friday, October 30, 2026, according to a report by TV BRICS, a media partner of the Agency of Nigeria (NAN).
Ethiopia Seeks to Expand Pharmaceutical Manufacturing in Africa
Argaw said Ethiopia was working towards building a pharmaceutical industry capable of meeting domestic healthcare needs and supplying products to other African countries.
The government intends to strengthen manufacturing capacity through regional partnerships, improved regulatory cooperation and coordinated purchasing arrangements.
According to the minister, producing more medical supplies within Africa is essential to ensuring that countries can respond effectively to public health challenges.
He identified medicines, vaccines and medical equipment as priority areas for expanding local production.
The strategy is expected to create opportunities for pharmaceutical companies, healthcare investors and manufacturers interested in developing production facilities and supply networks in Ethiopia.
AfCFTA to Support Ethiopia’s Pharmaceutical Industry
A major component of Ethiopia’s plan involves taking advantage of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
The trade agreement is designed to improve economic integration among African countries by reducing trade barriers and supporting the movement of goods and services across participating markets.
Argaw said Ethiopia intended to use the agreement to strengthen regional pharmaceutical supply chains and increase market access for medicines and other healthcare products manufactured in Africa.
The country also plans to encourage closer cooperation among regulatory authorities to make it easier for pharmaceutical manufacturers to operate across national borders.
Another priority is the introduction of joint procurement arrangements, under which participating countries or institutions could coordinate purchases of medicines and medical supplies.
Such arrangements could help manufacturers plan production around larger, more predictable orders.
Ethiopia Prioritises Local Vaccine and Medicine Production
The government believes that expanding domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing will play an important role in improving access to essential healthcare products.
Argaw stressed that African countries need stronger local production systems to reduce vulnerabilities associated with dependence on imported medicines and medical equipment.
The approach reflects growing interest across the continent in building pharmaceutical industries that can respond to public health emergencies and routine healthcare demands.
Ethiopia’s proposed strategy includes developing regional value chains, improving manufacturing capabilities and creating stronger links between producers, suppliers and healthcare institutions.
These efforts are intended to support a more reliable supply of medical products and strengthen the continent’s long-term health security.
Ethiopia’s Pharmaceutical Market Projected to Exceed $4 Billion by 2030
Ethiopia’s pharmaceutical market is projected to surpass $4 billion by 2030, according to the forecast cited in the TV BRICS report.
The projection highlights the scale of the market opportunity that Ethiopian authorities hope to support through investment and industrial development.
A growing pharmaceutical sector could attract manufacturers, encourage technology partnerships and create employment opportunities in medicine production, packaging, distribution and related services.
However, achieving the country’s ambitions will depend on factors including investment financing, reliable infrastructure, technical expertise, quality assurance and effective regulation.
The $4 billion figure represents a market forecast rather than confirmed investment or government funding.
Government Also Plans to Develop Medical Tourism
Alongside pharmaceutical manufacturing, Ethiopia is seeking to expand its medical tourism industry.
Argaw said the country intended to pursue opportunities in healthcare services for patients travelling from other countries.
The initiative could complement pharmaceutical development by strengthening healthcare infrastructure and encouraging investment in specialised medical services.
Medical tourism development may also create opportunities for hospitals, healthcare professionals and businesses providing related services.
The government has not disclosed specific investment targets, project locations or implementation deadlines for the medical tourism component of the strategy.
Ethiopia’s Ambition Reflects Africa’s Push for Health Security
Ethiopia’s pharmaceutical manufacturing plans come amid wider efforts by African governments and regional institutions to increase local production of healthcare products.
The COVID-19 pandemic exposed weaknesses in international medical supply chains and reinforced calls for stronger African manufacturing capacity.
Countries seeking to develop pharmaceutical industries face challenges involving financing, technology transfer, workforce development and regulatory compliance.
Ethiopia’s proposed use of AfCFTA, regional partnerships and joint procurement could help address some of these barriers if the measures are successfully implemented.
For the country, the ambition extends beyond supplying its domestic market to participating in a wider African pharmaceutical production and distribution network.
The success of the initiative will ultimately depend on how quickly the announced policies translate into operational manufacturing facilities, reliable supply chains and affordable healthcare products.

articles.title: Poland in political turmoil as Karol Nawrocki returns mid-flight amid Constitutional Court 'coup d'etat' claims. What's happening? - WION

Polish President Karol Nawrocki abruptly cancelled his visit to Africa while in mid-flight and returned to Warsaw on Friday as riot police were deployed around the country's Constitutional Court. The developments followed the suspension of the court's chief justice amid an escalating political confrontation between the centrist government and the nationalist right.
Dozens of police officers guarded the court's entrance as supporters of the opposition right-wing Law and Justice party (PiS) gathered to protest the removal of Constitutional Court President Bogdan Swieczkowski. The court's official account on X described the development as a 'coup d'etat', while some demonstrators chanted ‘Tusk traitor’ as they criticised Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government.
Several protesters held Roman Catholic rosaries and religious images while saying prayers. Police confirmed that three people had been arrested after attempting to enter the court complex. Tusk's government has been attempting for weeks to remove judges from the Constitutional Court who were appointed by the previous PiS administration, which governed Poland from 2015 to 2023. During that period, the court frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over European Union law. The EU accused Poland's highest court of being too closely aligned with the nationalist political authorities at the time.
🇵🇱 Police have moved onto the grounds of Poland's top court, and the president is flying home The court's chief was suspended tonight, and President Nawrocki turned his plane around mid-flight to Senegal. The court calls it a coup, while PM Tusk calls it "restoring the rule of law." Rule of law or power grab, what do you think? Writer: Daniyal https://t.co/SrVWTgNixh

Nawrocki returns amid political turmoil

Former PiS prime minister Jaroslaw Kaczynski addressed the demonstrators and urged Nawrocki to take action.
The president announced that he had cancelled his official visit to Senegal while already in the air and ordered his aircraft to return to Warsaw. According to media reports, he was expected to travel directly from the airport to the Constitutional Court. The suspension of Swieczkowski was announced by another judge, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who said the decision was necessary to restore the rule of law.
Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek, who also serves as attorney general, told journalists that he had requested the removal of the legal immunity of Swieczkowski and his deputy, Bartlomiej Sochanski. "This court has become private property; we must restore its proper functioning," he added. Tusk defended the government's actions in a post on X.
"Restoring the rule of law is our duty," he said. “After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.”
Conflict over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal escalates in Warsaw: judge suspends its leadership and president cuts short Africa trip A de facto power struggle has erupted within one of Poland’s most important state institutions in Warsaw today. For now, the outcome of this confrontation remains uncertain. Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska called the police to the grounds of the Constitutional Tribunal, citing a potential threat to the safety of judges and staff. Police did not enter the building, but a significant number of officers have been deployed in the surrounding area. Korwin-Piotrowska suspended Tribunal President Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, for one month, temporarily taking charge of the institution herself. Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, called the developments a “coup” and urged Polish President Karol Nawrocki to intervene. Nawrocki has cut short his visit to Senegal and is returning to Poland. The conflict stems from a deep division over the composition of the court. Donald Tusk’s government refuses to recognise the Tribunal’s rulings because of judges appointed under the previous PiS government. Meanwhile, Nawrocki and Święczkowski refuse to recognise judges elected by the Sejm in 2026. Korwin-Piotrowska is among them: the president refused to accept her oath of office, while Święczkowski had previously prevented her from participating in court proceedings.

Constitutional Court rejects suspension
The Constitutional Court's official website was inaccessible on Friday evening. Meanwhile, its official X account maintained that a 'coup d'etat' had taken place and insisted that Swieczkowski remained in office. The account also stated that Korwin-Piotrowska could not assume the role of interim chief justice because she had not been sworn in by the president. Amid the uncertainty surrounding the court's leadership, Korwin-Piotrowska defended the importance of the institution. "In modern Europe, a democratic state cannot function without a constitutional court (...) that acts as a guarantor of citizens' rights and freedoms."

On the sidelines of the recent IMF and World Bank annual meetings, one of the most notable reforms of the global debt architecture came from the establishment of a Borrowers Platform co-ordinated by the UN. The impetus for the platform came from the UN’s Fourth Financing for Development (FfD4) Conference in Seville, Spain, in 2025, agreed upon by all 190 countries.
The platform’s launch comes amid great strain on the global economy, with several internal and external factors exacerbating a debt and development crisis. High debt burdens are diverting public resources away from essential spending on public infrastructure and undermining growth. The external debt position of many developing countries is alarmingly high, with 54 countries, home to 3.4-billion people, spending more on servicing debt than on health or education.
The Borrowers Platform is styled as a permanent member state-led space to manage rising debt burdens by sharing knowledge, navigating debt renegotiations, improving data transparency, leveraging collective technical expertise, engaging in practical experiences and seeking solutions to common challenges developing countries face in the global debt architecture.
The platform also aims to strengthen the collective voice of developing countries to improve engagement with creditor groups that have long-standing institutions that co-ordinate positions, exchange information and develop common approaches such as in the Paris Club. The platform’s members have emphasised that it is not a crisis co-ordination mechanism, nor a forum for collective renegotiation of unsustainable debts.
Many countries that default are defaulting for the first time, with government officials who have little knowledge of the rules of the Paris Club debt restructuring game, with processes and rules that are often inadequately understood and applied inconsistently. The absence of a centralised legal framework (for instance, an international bankruptcy court) for sovereign debt leaves negotiations vulnerable to fragmentation, unpredictable litigation and isolated disputes.
Many countries that default are defaulting for the first time, with government officials who have little knowledge of the rules of the Paris Club debt restructuring game, with processes and rules that are often inadequately understood and applied inconsistently.
Stronger debt acquisition, management and resolution capabilities can send positive signals to creditors and credit rating agencies by reducing uncertainty, improving transparency and supporting more predictable debt outcomes, which may help lower the cost of capital over time.
The unfolding debt distress in Africa compelled South Africa to make debt sustainability for low-income countries one of its four presidential priorities in its 2025 G20 presidency. Despite debt distress being a stated priority and of keen interest to President Cyril Ramaphosa, progress on debt restructuring reform remained limited. Support for the Borrowers Platform is perhaps the only practical outcome on sovereign debt resolution coming out of South Africa’s G20 presidency, with Ramaphosa offering to convene the platform’s inaugural meeting in 2026.
Support for the Borrowers Platform by South Africa makes sense for five reasons related to existing commitments based on national values and interests:
- It would translate South Africa’s G20 commitment to solidarity and Ubuntu and the proposals of the African Expert Panel on Debt into a tangible institutional initiative.
- In a UN context, South Africa has supported the establishment of the platform.
- Regarding regional commitments, South Africa participated in the development of the Lome Declaration under the leadership of the AU Commission and the African Common Position on Debt (CAP) under the AU that called for reform of the G20 Common Framework and the establishment of a Borrowers Club.
- At a national level, support for the Global South and Africa in particular is embedded in South Africa’s foreign policy as outlined in the New Development Plan 2030, the Medium-Term Development Plan (MTDP), the constitution’s emphasis on human rights, and the Freedom Charter’s respect for sovereignty.
- Supporting technical and institution-building would contribute to stabilising fiscal positions and therefore political and economic stability in the region.
How South Africa positions itself in the international financial architecture has implications for its membership of the platform. In particular, taking up full membership of the Paris Club would limit its ability to be a member of the Borrowers Platform.
In 2022 South Africa transitioned from being an ad hoc member of the Paris Club, which it has been since 2015, to a prospective member, with the opportunity to join as a full member. Prospective member status means South Africa is in the process of being integrated into a full member and is currently treated as a full member, with inclusion in all the Paris Club’s meetings. Prospective members are testing the waters and do not have an obligation to join as a full member.
A return to Paris Club ad hoc participant status will not harm South Africa’s interests while still allowing it to be a member of the Borrower’s Platform. Ad hoc participant status allows participation in official creditor committees on a case-by-case basis when it has creditor exposure in a given default and allows South Africa to champion the issue of debt distress in Africa and the Global South through the Borrowers Platform.
This is a neutral move aligning with the Group of 77 developing countries broadly and would not aggravate Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) creditor countries given that there are already a number of countries with this status. OECD countries will also come to appreciate the role South Africa is playing in reducing default risks along the debt cycle, which is in their interests as creditors.
South Africa should become a leading supporter of the Borrowers Platform consistent with its international commitments, its aspiration to exercise constructive leadership on the continent, and its broader objective of strengthening the voice and agency of developing countries.
- Ramburuth, a researcher in sovereign debt and development finance at the Institute for Economic Justice, leads the institute’s global economic governance project
