SA Business Leaders Asks a $16 Billion Question: Will Washington Cut South Africa Out of AGOA Before Christmas?
27 October 2026
SACCUSA President Neil Diamond warns of possible AGOA exclusion and calls on the South African government to take urgent action to safeguard US market access and strengthen bilateral trade relations.
WASHINGTON D.C. — The South African Chamber of Commerce in the USA (SACCUSA) has issued an urgent warning to the South African government that the country faces a credible risk of losing its preferential trade benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), despite the recent extension of the program until December 2028.
SACCUSA President Mr Neil Diamond has called on the South African government to make the preservation of AGOA eligibility and the strengthening of US–South Africa trade relations an immediate national economic priority.
With approximately $16.5 billion in South African goods exported to the United States in 2025, the potential implications of exclusion extend well beyond preferential tariffs and could affect established commercial relationships, manufacturing investment, agricultural exports and employment opportunities.
“We are facing a $16 billion question that demands an urgent response from the South African government. Will Washington cut South Africa out of AGOA before Christmas, or can we demonstrate that maintaining and strengthening this trading relationship serves the economic interests of both countries?
South Africa cannot afford to approach this situation with complacency. The government must urgently engage Washington with a credible, commercially focused strategy that addresses American trade priorities and protects our access to the US market.”
— Neil Diamond, President, SACCUSA
A critical deadline demands immediate attention
On 2 September 2026, President Donald Trump signed legislation extending AGOA through 31 December 2028, following strong bipartisan congressional support for continued preferential trade with eligible African countries.
However, the extension does not guarantee South Africa’s continued participation. The US administration retains the authority to review countries’ eligibility and withdraw AGOA benefits in accordance with statutory requirements.
For an annual-review termination to become effective on 1 January 2027, the United States must provide at least 60 days’ advance notification, placing the relevant deadline at approximately 2 November 2026.
Although South Africa remains listed as an AGOA-eligible beneficiary as of 26 October, the approaching deadline creates significant uncertainty for exporters, investors and businesses operating between the two countries.
“Hope is not a trade strategy,” Diamond warned.
“South Africa must prepare for the possibility of exclusion, but our first priority must be to prevent that outcome. This requires urgent high-level engagement, clear commitments and a practical understanding of what Washington expects from its trading partners.”
A bilateral relationship worth protecting
According to the Office of the United States Trade Representative, bilateral trade in goods and services between South Africa and the United States reached approximately $28.8 billion in 2025, an increase of 10.1% over the previous year.
South African merchandise exports to the United States totaled approximately $16.5 billion, while American goods exports to South Africa reached approximately $6.3 billion. Bilateral services trade accounted for approximately $6 billion.
Although only a portion of South Africa’s exports receive AGOA preferences, the program remains important to sectors including automotive manufacturing, agriculture and specialized industrial production.
Potential exclusion would add pressure to businesses already navigating changes in American tariff policy, with possible consequences for export competitiveness, supply chains, investment decisions and employment.
American importers, manufacturers and distributors that rely on established South African suppliers could also be affected.
“The economic relationship between our countries is too important to place at unnecessary risk,” Diamond said.
“This is not simply about protecting South African exports. It is about preserving commercial relationships that have taken decades to develop and ensuring that American businesses continue to see South Africa as a dependable and competitive trading partner.”
South Africa must respond to American economic priorities
SACCUSA believes the South African government must approach negotiations with Washington from a practical commercial perspective, recognizing the Trump administration’s emphasis on reciprocal trade, expanding American exports, domestic manufacturing, strategic supply chains and investment opportunities.
Diamond cautioned that South Africa cannot rely solely on its historic participation in AGOA or assume that preferential market access will continue without addressing the concerns of the US administration.
“South Africa must make a stronger economic case for its relationship with the United States. We cannot simply ask Washington to preserve trade preferences. We must demonstrate how our partnership creates opportunities for American exporters, American investors and American businesses,” Diamond said.
“That means identifying opportunities to purchase more American goods and services, attract additional US investment and establish commercially sustainable partnerships that benefit both economies.”
SACCUSA believes opportunities exist to expand American exports of agricultural equipment, industrial machinery, technology, energy products and professional services to South Africa.
Similarly, American companies could benefit from additional investment opportunities in South African manufacturing, infrastructure, critical minerals, technology and energy.A renewed emphasis on reciprocal trade would strengthen the economic rationale for maintaining South Africa’s place within the broader US–Africa commercial relationship.
SACCUSA calls on the South African government to act
SACCUSA is calling on the Presidency, the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (DTIC), and the Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) to coordinate an urgent economic engagement strategy with Washington.
The Chamber believes the government should immediately prioritize the following actions:
1. Seek clarity from Washington: Engage the US administration at the highest appropriate level to establish the specific concerns affecting South Africa’s eligibility and identify practical measures that could preserve its participation in AGOA.
2. Present a credible reciprocal trade proposal: Identify opportunities to increase American exports to South Africa, reduce commercial barriers and demonstrate measurable benefits for US businesses and workers.
3. Mobilize private-sector participation: Involve South African and American business chambers, manufacturers, exporters, investors and industry associations in developing practical commercial solutions.
4. Strengthen engagement with Congress and US trade institutions: Work through established diplomatic and commercial channels to communicate the importance of bilateral trade and investment to both economies.
5. Prepare an immediate business contingency framework: Assist exporters and investors in assessing tariff exposure, contractual risks and potential supply-chain disruptions should South Africa’s eligibility change.
Diamond emphasized that these initiatives must be pursued as part of a coordinated national economic strategy rather than as isolated diplomatic interventions.
“The South African government must recognize that the preservation of our American market access is an economic priority, not merely a diplomatic matter,” he said.
“We need clear leadership, coordinated engagement and a commercially credible proposal that demonstrates South Africa’s willingness to strengthen reciprocal trade with the United States.”
US-based South African businesses stand ready to support engagement
SACCUSA believes South African business leaders operating in the United States have an important role to play in strengthening bilateral economic relations.
Through established commercial networks, business partnerships and engagement with American institutions, the Chamber seeks to support constructive dialogue and identify opportunities to expand trade and investment.SACCUSA encourages the South African government to draw upon the expertise and networks of South African businesses operating in the United States when developing its approach to Washington.
“South African business leaders in America understand the US commercial environment and recognize the importance of building relationships that deliver tangible benefits to American businesses,” Diamond said.
“We stand ready to support meaningful business engagement, strengthen commercial partnerships and contribute to a practical strategy that protects and expands the economic relationship between our countries.”
The time for decisive action is now
SACCUSA believes South Africa still has an opportunity to strengthen its economic relationship with the United States, but the approaching AGOA eligibility deadline requires immediate attention.
The Chamber cautions that uncertainty surrounding market access can discourage investment, delay business expansion and undermine confidence in established supply chains.

articles.summary: GDP tops forecasts on AI chip-led exports  The Star
articles.full_text:
SEOUL: South Korea’s economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter (3Q) as a global artificial intelligence (AI) chip boom boosted exports and investments, advance central bank estimates has showed, though domestic demand has remained weak.
Gross domestic product (GDP) expanded 1% in the July to September quarter from the preceding three months, when it grew 0.6%. It was stronger than a median 0.7% increase tipped in a Reuters poll of economists.
It was also higher than the Bank of Korea’s (BoK) forecast of 0.3% in August, when the central bank projected this year’s growth at 3.3%. The economy is now seen growing 3.7% this year, if GDP in the 4Q stays at the same level as the 3Q.
“It is estimated that half of economic growth is being driven by semiconductors,” Lee Dong-won, director general of BoK economic statistics department said.
Exports and investments are expected to remain robust in the 4Q, Lee said, adding that chip production volume will expand further next year while prices will continue to grow but at a slower pace.
Private consumption – which fell for the first time in nearly four years in the 3Q – will likely recover, as dividend payouts by chip firms to their shareholders in the 4Q and bonus payments to employees in the 1Q of 2027 boost household income, Lee said.
Amid the global boom in AI investment, South Korea’s exports topped US$800bil in January to September, higher than last year’s full-year record, and are on track to exceed US$1 trillion this year.
This will make South Korea the fourth country to reach the milestone, after the United States, China and Germany.
The central bank kept interest rates unchanged last week, after back-to-back hikes in July and September, but maintained a hawkish stance by upgrading its economic growth forecasts and remaining upbeat about the country’s export momentum.
“Exports and investments are leading growth, but the downside is that private consumption remains weak compared with the overall growth momentum,” said Park Sang-hyun, an economist at iM Securities.
“There could be short-term boosts, but it is difficult to expect strong momentum given labour market conditions and restrictive interest rates,” Park said.
In a BoK survey released last Thursday, consumer sentiment fell slightly in October, as the outlook for household income and consumer spending weakened.
In the 3Q, exports rose 2.3% on demand for semiconductors, machinery and electric equipment, while imports grew 2.4%.
Facilities investment jumped 4.1%, led by machinery such as semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Private consumption fell 0.2% as financial services declined on a stock market slump and car purchases fell due to strikes at major automakers.
On a year-on-year basis, GDP grew 3.4%, after rising 3.7% in the quarter before, also stronger than economists’ expectations for a 3% increase. — Reuters

The Pan-African Manufacturers Association (PAMA), has called on African governments and regional institutions to institutionalise private-sector participation in the negotiation, implementation and review of economic agreements.
The Association said Africa has built an extensive network of bilateral and multilateral economic relationships, including the EU-Africa partnership, Forum on China-Africa Cooperation and Africa-India engagement, as well as regional arrangements under the African Continental Free Trade Area, AfCFTA, but their industrial impact depends on how well they reflect commercial realities.
PAMA noted that while governments and regional institutions have the mandate to negotiate and conclude international agreements, businesses are the eventual users of many of their economic provisions.
“Governments and regional institutions have the mandate to negotiate and conclude international agreements, but businesses are the eventual users of many of their economic provisions. Manufacturers, investors and other private-sector operators understand the commercial conditions required to use market access, invest, source inputs and build cross-border operations,” the Association stated.
It observed that business membership organisations are often brought into the process after major negotiating positions have been established, leaving important commercial considerations outside the design of agreements.
According to PAMA, economic agreements should be designed with implementation in mind, as commitments on market access, investment, standards and cooperation have greater industrial value when they reflect conditions under which businesses can actually operate.
The Association said this requires structured consultation before agreements are concluded, followed by mechanisms through which business organisations can monitor implementation and identify emerging barriers.
“For manufacturers, the practical value of an agreement is determined by the extent to which its provisions can be converted into investment, production and trade,” it said.

articles.title: Putin Says Sanctions Make Moving Production to Africa Attractive - Kyiv Post
articles.summary: Putin Says Sanctions Make Moving Production to Africa Attractive  Kyiv Post
articles.full_text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, Oct. 29, said that Russian companies are interested in moving some production to African countries, explicitly linking the proposal to sanctions against Russia’s economy and businesses.
Speaking at the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, Putin endorsed closer industrial cooperation, according to the Kremlin’s transcript.
“Our companies are simply interested in moving certain production operations to African countries,” he said.
Putin described such cooperation as fully consistent with Russia’s interests, particularly while its companies face numerous sanctions. He also said Russian businesses had substantial investment potential.
However, he called on African governments to ensure that their decisions remained sovereign and that Russian investments were protected against changes in the international political environment.
His remarks did not identify particular factories, destination countries, or a timetable for relocating production.
African leaders seek production and investment
Putin was responding to Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who also chairs the African Union.
Ndayishimiye argued that Africa should move beyond exporting raw materials and importing finished goods. He called for investment in local manufacturing, modern agriculture, energy infrastructure, transport links, research, and technology.
He also urged Russian companies to invest more in African economies and help develop production and supply chains on the continent. Putin said the priorities outlined by the Burundian leader aligned with Moscow’s interests.
The two-day summit, held on Oct. 28-29, brought delegations from 48 African countries to Moscow, including 22 represented by their heads of state. The gathering is the third Russia-Africa summit, following meetings in 2019 and 2023.
Putin said Russia’s trade with African countries exceeded $27 billion in 2025. He presented energy, mining, industrial cooperation, and logistics as areas where Russian businesses were already pursuing major projects.
Russian companies pitch mining and energy projects
Russian officials and companies have used the gathering to promote cooperation across several industries.
Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov proposed partnerships in pharmaceuticals and information technology, while Industry and Trade Minister Anton Alikhanov outlined opportunities in vehicle manufacturing, The Moscow Times reported.
State nuclear corporation Rosatom proposed floating nuclear power plants for coastal African countries. Gas producer Novatek offered technology developed for its Russian liquefied natural gas projects.
Separately, aluminum producer Rusal signed a memorandum on a proposed joint venture to mine and process bauxite in Ghana, Reuters reported, citing Russian state news agency RIA.
The agreement concerns bauxite – the raw material used to produce aluminum. It represents a proposed investment project rather than confirmation that an existing Russian factory will be relocated.
Economic outreach accompanies military ties
Moscow’s investment pitch forms part of its wider effort to strengthen relationships with African governments as it faces Western pressure over its war against Ukraine.
The summit also provides a platform for Russian arms exports. State weapons exporter Rosoboronexport announced plans to present its “Anti-Drone Dome” system, combining detection equipment, electronic jamming, weapons, and physical barriers.
The company said the system could protect industrial facilities, energy infrastructure, buildings, and transport convoys. Its claims of effectiveness have not been independently verified.
In June, Andrii Cherniak, a representative of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR), said Moscow seeks resources and sanctions-evasion opportunities across the continent, alongside diplomatic support and recruits for its war.
He said Russia had maintained much of its military presence by reorganizing former Wagner operations under the defense ministry-backed Africa Corps, with forces supporting governments and armed groups in countries including Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso.
Cherniak also said Moscow uses African networks to obtain technologies for weapons production and expand its political influence through intelligence operations and organizations operating under civilian cover.

articles.title: Pretoria urges US talks as Agoa decision looms - IOL
articles.summary: Pretoria urges US talks as Agoa decision looms  IOL
articles.full_text:
SOUTH Africa’s ambassador to the United States, Roelf Meyer, has called for “direct dialogue” with Washington to break a diplomatic stalemate, as Pretoria prepares for the possibility of losing duty-free access to the US market under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa).
“The situation is tense and there’s a bit of a stalemate,” Meyer told AFP this week. “My view is that it can be addressed if there is direct dialogue between the US and South African authorities, and we hope we can establish that.”
Meyer said talks on Agoa could help ensure that “the right facts” reach US decision-makers “before decisions are being taken”. He said: “We have to be able to sit down and put the facts on the table.”
South Africa is Agoa’s largest beneficiary. The programme, which gives eligible sub-Saharan African countries preferential access to the US market, has been renewed until the end of 2028, but the US president reviews countries’ eligibility annually.
President Cyril Ramaphosa recently warned that exclusion would be “devastating”, while urging South Africans to prepare for the possibility. “Congress has decided that we should be kept in Agoa. What now remains is the executive,” he said.
Ramaphosa said the government would seek alternative markets if exclusion occurred. “I need as president to prepare us if it ever happens. So we should not go out and jump off tall buildings and think that this is the end of the world,” he said.
Relations have deteriorated since Donald Trump returned to office. Washington has cut aid, expelled South Africa’s previous ambassador and publicly criticised Ramaphosa over discredited claims of a “white genocide”, allegations Pretoria rejects.
In September, Washington also announced visa restrictions targeting South Africans it wrongly accused of promoting “race-based discrimination”, inciting violence or enabling land confiscation without compensation—issues South Africa disputes.
The standoff has extended to the G20. Washington has refused to accredit Pretoria for G20 meetings in the US, including December’s leaders’ summit.
Meyer said he would not assign blame for the deterioration but saw repairing the relationship as his responsibility. “I’m not going to put blame anywhere. It’s not necessary. I have a job to do, and that is to make sure that we restore the relationship in the best possible way and as quickly as we can.”
Meyer stressed the economic importance of the relationship, noting that more than 600 US companies operate in South Africa. “Trade relations [were] going on mostly as more than 600 US companies are doing business in South Africa to our benefit, because they provide jobs.
“We have to improve the relations at trade level; it is necessary, but also at a political level. We can’t go on like this,” he said. “Whether there’s persuasion necessary on the US side or on the South African side, I will be the messenger to try and make it happen.”
Although South Africa has been excluded from official US-hosted G20 meetings, Meyer confirmed that Pretoria had been invited to the B20, the G20’s business forum, in Washington next month.
“That is going ahead … we have been invited to be there, but it’s organised by business,” he said. “We will have business representatives at the B20, and as an embassy, we will participate in the B20.”
Meyer said South Africa should not allow itself to become a “political football,” but should put national interests first. “We must put that first in all our deliberations and in what we are trying to convey,” he said.
AFP reported that any US decision to remove South Africa from Agoa would require 60 days’ notice to Congress and to South Africa. For an exclusion to take effect on 1 January, it would need to be announced by 2 November.
Meyer’s call for direct talks reflects South Africa’s central argument: That a decision with major consequences for jobs and exports should be based on verified facts and formal engagement, not political rhetoric.

articles.title: ‘Logistics can contribute more to GDP than oil’ - The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.summary: ‘Logistics can contribute more to GDP than oil’  The Guardian Nigeria News

Nigeria’s courier, logistics, transport and management sector could contribute more to the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) than the oil and gas industry if its economic potential is fully harnessed, the Courier and Logistics Management Institute (CLMI) has said.
The institute said improved logistics infrastructure, skills development and technology adoption could strengthen agricultural value chains, expand non-oil exports, create jobs and generate significant revenue for the economy.
Executive Chairman of CLMI, Professor Simon Emeje, stated this ahead of the institute’s 2026 International Conference and Investiture, scheduled to hold on November 26 at the Oriental Hotel, Lagos.
The conference, themed: “Powering African Trade and Agricultural Entrepreneurship through Smart Logistics,” is expected to bring together stakeholders across logistics, agriculture, trade, investment and entrepreneurship to examine how efficient supply chains can improve Nigeria’s competitiveness.
Former President Olusegun Obasanjo will chair the event, while Hon. Ahmed Yakasi, former president of the Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria, will deliver the keynote address.
Emeje said the sector remained underutilised despite its potential to support economic diversification, reduce poverty and generate employment, arguing that the country needed to address skills gaps and better integrate logistics into its economic development plans.
“There are jobs in Nigeria; what is lacking is skills,” he said, adding that the institute was working to refocus economic thinking and promote a stronger role for logistics in Africa’s development.
According to him, logistics extends beyond the movement of goods to underpin government administration, political activities, commerce and the delivery of essential services.
He said the institute was engaging international partners and other stakeholders to promote practical solutions to supply-chain challenges, particularly those affecting agricultural production, distribution and exports.
Emeje cited Obasanjo’s position that Africa would struggle to expand trade without efficient logistics systems, noting that the movement of goods from farms to markets, manufacturers to consumers, and local businesses to international markets depended on reliable supply chains.
The conference, he said, would examine how technology-driven logistics could help African businesses overcome distribution bottlenecks, reduce costs and compete more effectively in global markets.
The CLMI chairman also stressed the need to expose young people to opportunities in courier services, logistics, transport and management. He said the institute was collaborating with universities to encourage innovation and develop the skills required by the industry.
He added that the conference was timely as Nigeria sought to increase non-oil exports and reduce its dependence on imports. According to him, exporters need a better understanding of logistics requirements across the value chain, while policymakers must engage industry operators to develop policies that address operational challenges.
Emeje expressed the hope that the conference communiqué would provide recommendations to support the sector’s growth and strengthen its contribution to economic diversification.

articles.title: Ethiopia Clears Another WTO Accession Hurdle with Canada Trade Deal - Birr Metrics
articles.summary: Ethiopia Clears Another WTO Accession Hurdle with Canada Trade Deal  Birr Metrics
articles.full_text:
Bilateral agreement concludes trade negotiations with Canada as Ethiopia prepares for its eighth WTO accession meeting in November.
Ethiopia has concluded bilateral market access negotiations with Canada, signing an agreement in Geneva as the country moves towards the next stage of its longstanding bid to join the World Trade Organization (WTO).
The agreement, signed on October 27 at the WTO headquarters in Geneva, marks the formal conclusion of market access negotiations between the two countries under Ethiopia’s accession process.
The development comes less than two weeks before the eighth meeting of the WTO Working Party on Ethiopia’s accession, scheduled for November 9–10, 2026, when members are expected to review progress in the country's negotiations.
Bilateral market access agreements form part of the requirements for countries seeking WTO membership. Applicants must negotiate commitments on tariffs, services and other market access conditions with interested existing members, alongside broader negotiations on domestic trade regulations and compliance with WTO rules.
The agreement with Canada represents progress on the bilateral component of Ethiopia’s accession negotiations, although the country must still complete the remaining multilateral and bilateral requirements before membership can be approved.
Speaking at the signing ceremony, Tsegab Kebebew, Ethiopia’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations and other international organisations in Geneva, said the agreement would strengthen commercial relations between the two countries.
He also linked the negotiations to Ethiopia’s broader economic reform programme, which includes changes to foreign exchange management, investment regulations and the country's trade framework.
According to Ethiopian officials, the agreement is expected to support trade and investment cooperation in agriculture, manufacturing, mining, renewable energy and logistics.
However, the announcement did not disclose the specific tariff commitments, services market access provisions or implementation arrangements agreed between the two governments.
Ethiopia's WTO accession process dates back to 2003, when the country formally applied to join the organisation. Negotiations have continued for more than two decades, with progress dependent on bilateral market access agreements and reforms to align domestic trade policies with international rules.
The government has placed WTO membership within its wider programme of macroeconomic and structural reforms, including measures introduced since July 2024 to liberalise the foreign exchange market and expand private-sector participation in the economy.
Accession would bring Ethiopia under the WTO's multilateral framework governing international trade, including rules on tariffs, trade transparency, services and dispute settlement.
For Ethiopia, bilateral negotiations with existing WTO members are particularly relevant because the commitments agreed during accession can determine the conditions under which foreign goods and service providers enter the domestic market.
The agreement with Canada also comes as Ethiopia seeks to expand international trade relationships and attract investment into sectors targeted under its economic reform programme.
Canada and Ethiopia have maintained diplomatic relations for approximately six decades, with cooperation spanning trade, development and investment.
The November Working Party meeting will provide the next formal opportunity for WTO members to assess Ethiopia's progress towards accession, including the status of bilateral negotiations and the country's domestic trade policy reforms.
While the agreement concludes negotiations with Canada, it does not constitute WTO membership. Ethiopia's accession will require the completion of outstanding negotiations and approval of its accession package under WTO procedures.

articles.title: Ruto courts Russian investors to narrow Kenya's trade gap - The Standard
articles.summary: Ruto courts Russian investors to narrow Kenya's trade gap  The Standard
articles.full_text:
President William Ruto is seeking Russian investment in Kenyan manufacturing and infrastructure as he attends the Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow.
Ruto departed Nairobi on Tuesday, October 27, for the summit and the accompanying Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum, scheduled for October 28 to 30.
Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi had travelled ahead of him.
                            
The summit brings together Russian and African leaders to discuss political cooperation, security, trade and economic development.
Kenya is using the engagement to seek wider markets for its exports and attract investment into local industries.
At a business roundtable in Moscow, Ruto said bilateral trade between Kenya and Russia stood at about Sh49.4 billion ($380 million) in 2025, with Kenya exporting goods worth Sh6.8 billion ($52 million) and importing Sh42.9 billion ($330 million).
He put Russian investment in Kenya at an estimated Sh2.9 billion ($22 million).
                            
Kenya’s trade statistics show that the country imported goods worth Sh33.33 billion from Russia in 2025 and exported goods worth Sh6.73 billion, leaving a trade deficit of Sh26.6 billion.
Ruto wants Russian companies to establish production facilities in Kenya, particularly in fertiliser manufacturing, mining, engineering, transport, agro-processing and irrigation.
He described Africa’s reliance on exporting raw materials and importing finished goods as “neither sustainable nor acceptable”, calling for greater value addition, local manufacturing, job creation and technology transfer.
The President argued that Kenya could serve as a production base for companies seeking access to the wider African market.
                            
Ruto said Kenya was mobilising Sh5.2 trillion ($40 billion) for infrastructure over the next decade, presenting the programme as an opportunity for private investors.
He pointed to the National Infrastructure Fund and urged Russian firms to consider opportunities in energy, transport and other infrastructure projects.
Renewable energy is another area Kenya is promoting. Ruto said 93 per cent of the country’s electricity comes from renewable sources and identified geothermal development, green hydrogen, electric mobility and energy infrastructure as potential investment areas.
He also cited Kenya’s population of about 55 million, its young workforce and its digital economy as advantages for investors.
Mobile money transactions exceeded Sh58.4 trillion ($450 billion) in 2025, according to figures in his statement.
He added that nearly 85 per cent of adults were financially included.
Ruto put Kenya’s gross domestic product at Sh17.7 trillion ($136 billion) and economic growth at 5.3 per cent in 2025.
Kenya targets wider African market
Ruto urged investors to look beyond Kenya’s domestic market and consider opportunities under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which aims to create a single market across the continent.
He said Kenya attracted Sh415.6 billion ($3.2 billion) in foreign direct investment in 2025, while East Africa received Sh1.95 trillion ($15 billion) and Africa Sh9.09 trillion ($70 billion).
United Nations Trade and Development (UNCTAD) reported that Africa received about Sh9.09 trillion ($70 billion) in foreign direct investment in 2025, down from Sh12.21 trillion ($94 billion) in 2024.
The continental figure was the third-highest annual total since 1990.
Kenya’s participation in the summit comes as the government seeks to diversify export markets and attract investment into sectors that can increase the value of locally produced goods.

articles.title: India FTA Tracker 2026: Live Updates on Trade & Economic Pacts - India Briefing
articles.summary: India FTA Tracker 2026: Live Updates on Trade & Economic Pacts  India Briefing
articles.full_text:
India’s foreign trade landscape in 2026 is being reshaped by a new generation of free trade agreements (FTAs) and a strategic push toward export market diversification.
A major milestone came in January 2026 with the conclusion of the India-European Union (EU) Free Trade Agreement, widely considered one of India’s most ambitious trade pacts to date. Once implemented, the agreement is expected to significantly deepen India’s integration with European markets, facilitate regulatory alignment, and strengthen participation in global supply chains spanning manufacturing, services, and digital trade.
The India FTA Tracker 2026 provides businesses and investors with a consolidated overview of India’s evolving trade architecture, highlighting the latest economic engagements, newly concluded agreements, ongoing negotiations, and regulatory developments shaping market access opportunities. For companies engaged in international trade, supply chain management, and cross-border investment, understanding these agreements is essential for navigating tariff benefits, rules of origin requirements, and emerging regulatory standards across India’s expanding trade corridors.
Optimise Trade Benefits
Assess tariff concessions, RoO requirements, market-access provisions, and tax implications across India’s international agreements.
Economic and trade engagements: October
India and Mexico sign terms of reference to begin trade negotiations
India and Mexico have signed the Terms of Reference (ToR) on 28 October 2026 to formally launch negotiations for a Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA). The proposed agreement aims to expand bilateral trade, promote investment, create business opportunities, and strengthen supply chain resilience. Negotiations will cover market access for goods, rules of origin, customs procedures, trade facilitation, and other key trade-related areas.
As per the central government, priority sectors for India-Mexico cooperation include automotive, chemicals, electronics, pharmaceuticals, agri-food, energy, critical minerals, and advanced manufacturing. Both countries are also considering a Mexican business mission to India in the first quarter of 2027 to facilitate business partnerships and identify commercial opportunities.
India-NZ FTA comes into effect
The free trade agreement between India and New Zealand is now in effect, carrying several advantages for both countries in terms of mobility, investments and exchange of goods. Under the pact, India gains duty-free access to 100 per cent of New Zealand’s tariff lines. In terms of the movement of natural persons, India now offers five temporary entry routes for New Zealand nationals, providing a wider net of opportunities for professionals to work in India with ease.
The agreement, signed on 24 April 2026, also includes New Zealand investment commitments of US$20 billion in India. Both countries have set a target of doubling bilateral trade in goods and services by 2030.

India-NZ FTA Rules of Origin notified on 12 October 2026
India has notified the Customs Tariff (Determination of Origin of Goods under the Free Trade Agreement between India and New Zealand) Rules, 2026, on 12 October 2026. The rules establish product-specific origin criteria, qualifying value content (QVC) requirements, and documentation procedures for claiming preferential customs duty treatment. They also allow qualifying goods to retain their originating status when shipped through third countries, subject to restrictions on further processing and continued customs control. The rules of origin will come into effect on 20 October 2026.
Economic and trade engagements: September
India-EU FTA to be signed on 16 December 2026
According to a report published by The Hindu on 24 September 2026, India and the European Union (EU) are expected to sign their Free Trade Agreement (FTA) on 16 December 2026. The agreement has reportedly secured “majority approval” in Europe and, subject to the European Council’s approval, would not require separate ratification by each EU member state.
Following the signing, the agreement will require approval by the European Parliament, a process expected to take another one to two months. This could pave the way for the FTA to become operational in early 2027.
India-New Zealand FTA to take effect on 20 October 2026
The central government has announced that the India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) will enter into force on 20 October 2026. The agreement aims to strengthen bilateral trade by providing preferential market access, facilitating US$20 billion in investment into India, and expanding opportunities in services and professional mobility.
Upon implementation, New Zealand will eliminate tariffs on 100 per cent of tariff lines covering India’s exports, granting Indian exporters duty-free access across all product categories. In return, India has offered tariff concessions on 70.03 percent of its tariff lines, covering approximately 95 per cent of the current bilateral trade value.
India has also undertaken market-access commitments across 106 service sectors and sub-sectors, including financial, telecommunications, environmental, and professional services. The agreement further provides for foreign commercial presence in specified financial services activities, with India allowing foreign direct investment (FDI) of up to 74 per cent in the insurance sector and foreign private-sector banks, subject to applicable conditions.
India-MERCOSUR
India and the MERCOSUR bloc signed the First Additional Protocol to their Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA) on 14 September 2026 to facilitate the use and acceptance of electronic Certificates of Origin (CoOs). Under the protocol, electronic CoOs will carry the same legal validity and evidentiary value as paper-based certificates, streamlining origin verification and documentation for preferential trade.
The protocol does not alter existing tariff concessions under the PTA. Instead, it modernises origin-certification procedures, supporting more efficient administration of preferential trade between India and MERCOSUR member countries.
Separately, India and MERCOSUR have initiated negotiations to expand the scope of their PTA, with the objective of creating additional trade and business opportunities for private-sector enterprises on both sides. The two parties are working to finalise the Terms of Reference (ToR), which will define the scope and framework for the proposed expansion.
18th BRICS Summit
The 18th BRICS Summit, held in New Delhi on 12-13 September 2026, marked the conclusion of India’s year-long BRICS chairship and culminated in the adoption of the New Delhi Declaration. The two-day summit addressed a broad range of economic cooperation priorities, including the Strategy for BRICS Economic Partnership 2030, cross-border payments, the proposed New Investment Platform, MSME financing, customs cooperation, resilient supply chains, and technology collaboration.
A key India-specific initiative discussed at the summit was the proposal to establish a BRICS Risk Lab at Gujarat’s GIFT City International Financial Services Centre (IFSC). The proposed facility is intended to support cooperation on risk assessment and related financial-sector capabilities within the BRICS framework.
Economic and Trade Engagements: August
India-Chile advance CEPA negotiations
India and Chile are advancing negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) to build on their existing PTA, in force since 2007 and expanded in 2017. On 26 August 2026, India’s Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal met Paula Estévez Weinstein, Vice-Minister of International Economic Relations of Chile, in Santiago to discuss progress on the proposed agreement.
The discussions highlighted opportunities to expand economic cooperation across key sectors, including healthcare, pharmaceuticals, energy, minerals, agriculture, machinery, and engineering. A successful conclusion of CEPA negotiations is expected to further strengthen the growing trade and economic partnership between the two countries.
India and SACU sign Terms of Reference (ToR) for PTA negotiations
On 12 August 2026, India and the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) signed the Terms of Reference (ToR) to initiate negotiations for a Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA). The proposed agreement aims to build on existing commercial ties by providing preferential market access and expanding trade opportunities across sectors with complementary strengths.
India’s Union Commerce Minister highlighted the country’s potential to support the SACU region through affordable medicines and IT-sector skill development. He also underscored opportunities to deepen cooperation in engineering goods, machinery, automobiles, pharmaceuticals, textiles, agriculture, and agri-processing. The negotiations seek to strengthen existing trade relations and unlock further opportunities for businesses across both regions.
Economic and Trade Engagements: July
India-UK CETA and Social Security Agreement enter into force
The India-United Kingdom Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), alongside the Agreement on Social Security, also known as the Double Contribution Convention (DCC), officially entered into force on 15 July 2026.
Under CETA, Indian businesses gain preferential, including duty-free, access to approximately 99 per cent of UK tariff lines, covering nearly all Indian exports to the UK. articles.title: Ethiopia, Russia Strengthen Nuclear Energy Partnership As Abiy Announces Plans For Power Plant - Trendsnafrica
articles.summary: Ethiopia, Russia Strengthen Nuclear Energy Partnership As Abiy Announces Plans For Power Plant  Trendsnafrica
articles.full_text:
(3 Minutes Read)
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced on Thursday that Ethiopia is moving forward with plans to partner with Russia to develop a nuclear power plant, a proposed initiative that could mark a significant step in the country’s efforts to diversify its energy sources and strengthen its long-term electricity supply.
Speaking at the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, Abiy highlighted the importance of expanding bilateral cooperation in energy, technology and economic development. He said the proposed nuclear power project reflects the two countries’ shared interest in strengthening their strategic partnership and translating diplomatic commitments into tangible development outcomes. In a statement shared on social media, the Ethiopian leader stressed that sustained cooperation and collective commitment would be essential to implementing the agreements reached during the summit. He underscored the need to ensure that discussions between the two governments lead to practical results that contribute to Ethiopia’s national development priorities.
Abiy identified food security and agricultural productivity, reliable energy supplies, and the transfer of skills and knowledge as three central pillars of Ethiopia’s development strategy. According to him, progress in these areas will be essential to achieving sustainable prosperity, improving economic productivity and supporting the country’s broader transformation agenda.
The proposed nuclear power plant forms part of Ethiopia’s wider efforts to diversify its energy mix and meet rising electricity demand. The country has invested heavily in expanding its power-generation capacity, with hydropower remaining a central component of its electricity system. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), one of Africa’s largest hydropower projects, represents a major element of these efforts. However, as Ethiopia pursues industrial expansion, urban development and improved electricity access, diversifying its generation sources could help strengthen the resilience and reliability of its power system.
Nuclear energy can provide continuous electricity generation, making it a potential source of stable baseload power for energy-intensive industries, manufacturing facilities and other major consumers. If implemented, the proposed project could complement Ethiopia’s existing renewable energy resources while supporting its long-term ambitions to expand industrial production and strengthen economic competitiveness.
However, developing a nuclear power programme would require substantial investment, advanced technical expertise, robust regulatory institutions, skilled personnel and comprehensive safety and waste-management systems. The project’s eventual contribution to Ethiopia’s energy sector would depend on its financing, technical arrangements, implementation timeline and regulatory preparedness.
The announcement also underscores the longstanding relationship between Ethiopia and Russia, which dates back more than 120 years. Over the decades, the two countries have maintained diplomatic and cultural exchanges, providing a foundation for cooperation in areas such as education, technology, trade and economic development.
Abiy described the relationship as one built on mutual respect and shared benefits, indicating that the proposed nuclear energy initiative could open additional avenues for collaboration. For Russia, cooperation with Ethiopia could provide an opportunity to expand its engagement with African countries in the energy and technology sectors. For Ethiopia, a partnership with Russian institutions could potentially facilitate access to nuclear technology, technical training and specialised expertise needed to establish a civilian nuclear energy programme. The initiative therefore reflects a broader pattern of cooperation between African governments and international partners seeking to develop infrastructure, strengthen energy security and support economic growth through technological investment.
If realised, Ethiopia’s nuclear power project could place the country among a relatively small group of African nations pursuing nuclear energy as part of their long-term development strategies. It could also contribute to wider discussions across East Africa about how to meet increasing electricity demand while supporting industrialisation and economic growth.
Reliable and affordable electricity is widely recognised as an important requirement for expanding manufacturing, improving public services and attracting investment. Diversifying power generation could help Ethiopia manage future demand and reduce its reliance on a limited number of energy sources, although the scale of these benefits would depend on the project’s eventual capacity and cost.
Nevertheless, the announcement represents a proposed development rather than evidence that a nuclear power plant is already under construction. Further details regarding the project’s financing, location, generating capacity, construction schedule and regulatory framework would be needed to establish its scope and likely impact.

South Africa's Economy 4.9% Larger After GDP Rebasing, Stats SA Says
South Africa's economy was estimated to be 4.9% larger than previously reported following a benchmarking and rebasing exercise, according to Statistics South Africa. The statistics agency said on Thursday that the exercise raised the size of the economy in 2022 to 6.99 trillion rand, equivalent to $420.19 billion, from a previously published estimate of 6.67 trillion rand.
The agency changed the base year for its gross domestic product estimates to 2022 from 2015. It also accounted for shifts in the composition of the formal and informal parts of the economy.
All 10 sectors tracked by the agency showed higher output. Mining, finance and trade recorded the largest increases, partly because illicit or illegal activity in those industries was factored in.
In nominal terms, GDP for last year was revised to 8.04 trillion rand from 7.64 trillion rand. The rand conversion rate cited was 16.6354 per dollar.

articles.full_text:
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin speaks during the plenary session of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, held in the presence of President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and many African leaders and officials.
MOSCOW – 29 October 2026: Russia’s President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that the Russian ruble has accounted for up to 85% of commercial transactions between Russia and African countries, according to Russian reports.
Speaking while chairing the plenary session of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, Putin said Russia and Africa shared strong bonds of friendship and close partnership, describing them as natural allies in building a multipolar and democratic world order.
He highlighted that this order is “free from dictates and double standards and is based on respect for international law and the fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter.”
Putin also said Russian businesses dealt with their African partners with honesty, respect, and responsibility, operating on an equal footing rather than pursuing profits through practices reminiscent of those of former colonial powers.
Instead, he said, Russian companies invested and reinvested their returns in developing African countries’ economies.
Third Russia-Africa Summit
The Russia-Africa Summit is a major forum for strengthening cooperation between Russia and African countries across political, security, economic, scientific, technological, cultural, and humanitarian fields.
President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi arrived in Moscow on Tuesday to lead Egypt's delegation to the summit for the third time.
On the sidelines of the summit, El-Sisi also held talks with Putin, where they discussed deepening their strategic relations and exchanged views on regional tensions.
The third edition of the summit, co-chaired by Putin and Burundian President and African Union Chairperson Évariste Ndayishimiye, is being held in Moscow on October 28–29, 2026.
It brings together representatives of nearly 50 African countries, including heads of state and government, according to the Russia Foreign Ministry.
Participants will discuss expanding ties in trade, investment, science, technology, and other areas.
The summit is expected to adopt a final declaration, a 2027–2029 action plan for the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum, a declaration on cooperation in the civilian use of AI, and a package of intergovernmental and interdepartmental agreements.

articles.title: Under the hood of the energy transition - Mining.com.au
articles.summary: Under the hood of the energy transition  Mining.com.au
articles.full_text:
Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, a global leader in electric vehicle (EV) and battery supply chain research, published its report on September 2026 EV sales, noting a 17% month-on-month increase despite a 2% year-on-year decrease.
The month saw 2.15 million EVs sold globally, led by the UK and Europe, while North America and China saw slowdowns.
Benchmark reports that Europe and the UK saw their strongest month on record, with nearly 600,000 EVs sold. Sales were up 39% year-on-year, led by battery EVs, followed by plug-in hybrids.
The growth across the region was broad, spanning the UK, France, Spain, Portugal, and Finland, with each country recording its highest-ever monthly EV sales.
September 2026 also saw the European Union (EU) and China agree to limit the imports of Chinese-built hybrids into the region to 350,000 units a year for four years from 2027.
According to Benchmark, around 14% of plug-in hybrid EVs sold in the UK, EU, and European Free Trade Association in 2025 were made in China, with that number rising to 29% in 2026.
Higher fuel prices, driven by the war in Iran, have in fact encouraged more EV purchases throughout the region.
North America’s decline was steep, down 44% year-on-year in September. Benchmark’s report notes that this decline reflects a comparison to September 2025, which saw record growth as US buyers rushed to purchase EVs before the expiry of the federal government’s tax credit.
The authors note that they expect the decline to narrow moving forward, as new figures will be measured against the months following the removal of the tax credit.
Notably, China’s EV sales declined 18% year-on-year in September, even as sales rose 7% month-on-month. That said, EV penetration across China remains strong. While domestic demand was down, manufacturers were able to maintain production and exports to other markets.
EV exports out of China reached a monthly record of 558,000 units in September, though policy changes, such as those out of the EU, could impact those figures moving forward.
China drives the global EV market
Wood Mackenzie notes that overall, the industry is trending up, with EVs now representing one in three new cars sold globally, despite the regional complexities.
The analytics and data company notes that Chinese-made EVs are setting a new benchmark for affordability, even if that’s not helping to turn around domestic sales. While Chinese EV penetration is at nearly 70%, sales are down nearly 1 million units since the 2025 peak of 9 million.
Wood Mackenzie notes that it’s not just EVs, but China’s entire vehicle market that’s seeing lower sales this year, with internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles accounting for the biggest drop in sales, mostly driven by a weak macroeconomic outlook.
While Chinese consumers may be buying fewer vehicles, Chinese EVs are being exported to global markets in larger numbers, with buyers noting that the prices are more competitive than Western-made EVs.
With Europe setting import quotas on Chinese EVs, Chinese automotive manufacturers are building capacity and battery supply chains within Europe itself, providing a new market for European-made Chinese EVs to replace those imports.
The critical metals behind every EV
Compared to ICE vehicles, EVs require a wider range of metals and significantly greater volumes overall.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) notes that an ICE vehicle requires around 22.3kg of copper (Cu), 11.2kg of manganese (Mn), 0.1kg of zinc, and 0.3kg of other metals.
Compare that to an EV, which contains 53.2kg Cu, 8.9kg of lithium, 39.9kg of nickel, 24.5kg Mn, 13.3kg of cobalt, 66.3kg of graphite, from 0.5 to 1kg of rare earths, 0.1kg of zinc, and 0.3kg of others.
Benchmark Head of Battery Raw Materials Adam Webb highlights that the same raw materials needed for EVs are also fuelling another fast-growing sector: battery energy storage systems (BESS).
The most important material Webb highlights is lithium, which is used across all lithium-ion batteries, with about 90% of lithium demand coming from the battery sector.
Webb notes that the lithium market has been in deficit this year, largely driven by the BESS sector rather than EVs.
“We’ve seen new BESS deployments increase by around 40% year-on-year. We’re expecting that this year, the supply of those batteries will increase at an even greater rate,” Webb says.
The growth in production of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries in particular has pushed demand up for lithium this year quite significantly, accounting for 30% of its growth.
On the supply side of lithium, there have been pockets of growth, with new projects coming online. This has pushed supply up around 20%, but it still does not keep pace with demand.
On the pricing front, the supply deficit has driven lithium carbonate prices up from about US$10,000 ($14,173) per tonne in mid-2025 to above US$20,000. Webb notes that while there’s been a recent pullback in prices, that’s more sentiment-driven, as the fundamentals still point to a supply deficit.
Nickel and cobalt are both used in the cathode of nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) batteries, which are not used in the BESS sector but are prevalent in EVs.
Around 75% of mined cobalt supply comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The DRC has imposed export bans and quotas on copper and cobalt concentrates to encourage domestic processing and local value addition, as previously reported. This has reduced the amount of cobalt entering the market, pushing it into a deficit and driving a rally in prices.
Nickel has faced a similar situation, with Indonesia dominating the market and accounting for 60% of global supply. Indonesia has also imposed quotas through the Rencana Kerja dan Anggaran Biaya (RKAB) system, limiting the amount of ore that can be mined to supply its smelters.
With quotas much lower this year than in previous years, Indonesia’s output has been significantly affected, resulting in an overall drop in nickel production. At the same time, demand is rising from the battery and stainless steel markets.
Rare earth elements (REEs) too are essential, not just in EVs, but across renewable energies such as wind turbines, and in defence applications, including fighter jets, submarines, missiles, and radar.
Around 1kg of REEs is needed for an EV, while a 3 megawatt wind turbine uses 2 tonnes of rare earth magnets and a US F-35 fighter jet requires 920 pounds of REEs.
Building a rare earths and lithium future
Avalon Advanced Materials (TSX:AVL) is positioning itself as a key North American player in the energy transition through the sustainable development of lithium and REEs.
The company’s Nechalacho Project in Canada’s Northwest Territories is being advanced as a potential key supplier of magnet rare earth elements and other strategic materials to Western markets. China currently controls over 90% of total rare earth processing capacity.
Nechalacho provides exposure across terbium, dysprosium, praseodymium, and neodymium, key metals used in EVs, wind turbines, robotics, electronics, and in key defence technologies.
Avalon is taking a sustainable approach to rare earths processing, working in collaboration with Engina Corporation. Together, the companies have successfully recovered 15 REEs from Nechalacho concentrate, with over 90% total recovery in preliminary testing. This has been achieved using a CO2-based extraction process.
Avalon’s Lake Superior Lithium Project in Thunder Bay, Ontario, is a proposed lithium chemical processing facility that is looking to convert spodumene concentrate into battery-grade lithium for the BESS and EV sectors.
The company notes that demand for lithium is growing rapidly, with expectations that 96% of lithium demand will come from the battery space by 2040.
Avalon is advancing Lake Superior as an efficient and sustainable path to battery-grade lithium, using Metso’s (METSO.HE) proprietary alkaline leach process.
Avalon Advanced Materials is focused on securing and developing critical minerals projects to support domestic supply chains for the clean energy, advanced manufacturing, and technology sectors.
Backing battery-grade manganese
Black Canyon (ASX:BCA) is advancing ‘high-grade’ contained manganese deposits in Western Australia, including the Wandanya manganese and iron discovery.
The company notes the strategic nature of manganese, with the current supply chain mainly focused in South Africa, Gabon, and Australia. Manganese is essential in the production of steel, but has a growing role in lithium-ion battery cathodes, enhancing the energy density, capacity, and safety of the batteries while helping to reduce costs as compared to alternative chemistries that are high in cobalt.
Black Canyon has recently reported a maiden mineral resource estimate (MRE) for Wandanya, noting 23.6 million tonnes (Mt) at 25.8% Mn. The company is also expecting to complete its Scoping Study for the project by December 2026.
The resource at Wandanya comprises 66% measured, 26% indicated, and 8% inferred, at a 12% Mn cut-off. At higher cut-offs, the deposit contains 16.8Mt @ 30% Mn (20% cut-off) and potential direct ship ore material at 3.7Mt @ 38.9% Mn (35% cut-off).
Wandanya also contains a separate iron resource at 12.5Mt @ 54.9% iron.
Black Canyon is a Western Australian manganese explorer and developer, advancing the Wandanya Project in the Pilbara.
Chasing US lithium supply

The company is focused on the potential to supply high-purity, battery-grade lithium made in the US from Nevada’s ‘battery belt’.

articles.full_text:
A new energy center is emerging on the Mediterranean coast, and it's not in Europe. Morocco's $5.5 billion Nador West Med development could transform the kingdom's position in Mediterranean energy markets. More broadly, the project reflects the strategic vision of His Majesty King Mohammed VI, whose long-term approach to maritime infrastructure and industrial development has helped position Morocco as a major hub connecting Europe, Africa and international markets. While Nador West Med is often described as a new container port, its energy infrastructure may ultimately prove just as significant as its capacity to handle international shipping.
Under the King's leadership, Morocco anticipated the profound reshaping of global trade and value chains. Tanger Med, launched at His Majesty's initiative, demonstrated how investment in maritime infrastructure could attract international manufacturers, strengthen export industries and transform the country's economic position. Nador West Med represents the next chapter in that strategy, extending Morocco's maritime and industrial network along its Mediterranean coast while creating new opportunities in energy and logistics.
Located on Morocco's Mediterranean coast, Nador West Med will include a hydrocarbon terminal with a handling capacity of 25 million tonnes and storage capacity of 400,000 cubic meters. More significantly, the project includes a liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal designed to process 5 billion cubic meters annually. This is orders of magnitude larger than Morocco's annual demand.
The new facility could also support Europe's growing demand for LNG and emerging African suppliers, from Mauritania and Senegal to other markets in the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). By expanding its energy infrastructure, Morocco could strengthen its role as a link between European demand and developing African energy markets.
The LNG terminal represents a significant investment in Morocco's energy security. As electricity demand and industrial production increase, the capacity to import and store natural gas could provide greater flexibility in meeting the country's energy requirements.  
The terminal's proposed capacity should not, however, be confused with current Moroccan gas demand or guaranteed future throughput. Its ultimate commercial value will depend on implementation, market development and the country's evolving energy requirements.
On October 28, King Mohammed VI chaired a meeting to review progress at Nador West Med, with the first phase of its main container terminal approaching operation.
"Nador West Med (NWM) is set to complete the Tanger Med offer and significantly strengthen Morocco's logistical, industrial and energy positioning. The project, which combines port infrastructure with industrial, logistical and energy platforms, has to date mobilized 54 billion dirhams of public and private investment," the Royal Office stated.
For investors, the energy infrastructure creates opportunities in storage, terminal operations and associated logistics. It also supports Nador West Med's broader industrial ambitions by providing infrastructure manufacturers and other businesses will need as they establish operations around the port.
The project's significance extends beyond its immediate commercial potential. In line with the Crown's wider development priorities, its success will also be measured by whether investment translates into better living conditions, opportunities for young people and openings for local businesses. For the Oriental region, the challenge is to ensure that Nador West Med becomes a catalyst for wider economic development rather than an isolated center of prosperity.
Nador West Med is part of King Mohammed VI's broader strategy to position Morocco as a major maritime, industrial and logistics hub connecting Europe, Africa and international markets.

articles.title: Tinubu Defends Borrowing, Says Infrastructure Investments Will Create Jobs, Drive Economic Growth - Arise News
articles.summary: Tinubu Defends Borrowing, Says Infrastructure Investments Will Create Jobs, Drive Economic Growth  Arise News
articles.full_text:
President Bola Tinubu has issued an official response to critics, especially opposition leaders, of his government’s new loans from international institutions and banks.
In an essay, titled, “From reforms to delivery: Our infrastructure investment and growth strategy,” to be published on Nigerian news platforms, the president wrote, “The real question is not how much we borrow, but what we build, what value we create, and what future we leave behind.”
Tinubu identified the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, Sokoto-Badagry Superhighway, Trans-Sahara Superhighway, electricity grid upgrades, and the modernisation of key commercial ports in Lagos as major projects expected to strengthen Nigeria’s productive capacity.
The Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway is expected to cut logistics costs along its corridor by 15 to 20 per cent. It could add up to two per cent to Nigeria’s GDP through expanded trade, tourism, and industrial activity.
The project is also projected to generate about 100,000 direct jobs in construction and engineering, alongside more than 150,000 indirect jobs in logistics, materials, and related services.
According to the president, the projects, alongside investments in healthcare, education, and vocational training, would connect economic regions, reduce logistics costs, unlock agricultural and industrial potential, and attract private investment.
Tinubu disclosed, “We are not simply building highways. We are opening economic corridors, connecting markets, unlocking industries and reshaping Nigeria’s economic geography.”
He said the administration’s ambition to build a $1 trillion economy by 2030 would require sustained infrastructure investment to support higher productivity, industrialisation and trade.
“We cannot build a USD 1 trillion economy with infrastructure designed for an economy a fraction of that size,” Tinubu said.
He wrote that improving economic indicators and growing international investor confidence were creating opportunities for Nigeria to attract long-term investment and expand critical infrastructure.
The president said the economic reforms his administration introduced in May 2023 helped restore macroeconomic stability, strengthen public finances, and improve the country’s standing in international financial markets.
He said a $1 trillion economy would not emerge by declaration alone but must be built through sustained investment, higher productivity, industrialisation, and trade, stressing that infrastructure development would be critical to achieving the target by 2030.
Tinubu said real Gross Domestic Product growth reached 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, while headline inflation fell to 14.63 per cent in September, from 20.98 per cent a year earlier.
He also said gross external reserves rose to $55.1 billion as of October 9, 2026, including about $46 billion in net reserves, while the tax-to-GDP ratio increased to 12.5 per cent, from seven per cent.
The president attributed the improvements to measures, including petrol subsidy removal, exchange rate unification, tax reforms, and coordinated efforts to tackle inflation.
“The decisions taken since 2023 were difficult but necessary,” he said.
Tinubu said the gains had strengthened Nigeria’s ability to attract investment and finance projects that support long-term economic growth.
“Confidence has a price; our cost of borrowing is going down, and the country risk premium has drastically decreased,” he said.
The president cited positive assessments by international credit rating agencies as evidence of improved confidence in the economy.
He stated, “These are not political endorsements; they are independent assessments by global rating agencies, index providers, regulators and investors, recognising stronger external reserves, improved macroeconomic management and greater financial credibility.”
According to the president, the improved standing could help Nigeria attract more institutional investors, secure longer-term financing, and reduce borrowing costs.
He said the administration was shifting public borrowing away from financing short-term fiscal pressures towards investments that would generate economic returns, create jobs, and expand opportunities for future generations.
Tinubu said the government was also pursuing longer-term financing arrangements to match the lifespan of infrastructure assets, reduce refinancing pressures, and secure more competitive funding for productive investments.
He said Nigeria must convert renewed international confidence into capital expenditure, completed infrastructure, and lasting economic benefits for citizens.
He identified five priorities for the next phase of the Federal Executive Council’s economic strategy: food affordability and energy price stability, budget harmonisation and fiscal discipline. completion of high-impact projects and investment in critical infrastructure, an improved economic policy framework and regulatory efficiency, and targeted household support alongside investment in human development.
Tinubu stressed that the success of the current administration’s economic schemes would be measured by completed projects, increased investment, employment generation, and improved living standards.
He stated, “Securing financing is not the achievement. Completing the project, delivering value and improving the lives of Nigerians is the achievement.”
The president added that the country’s economic ambition must be supported by responsible borrowing and investments that create lasting opportunities for future generations.
Deji Elumoye
