articles.title: From Subsidy Politics to Infrastructure-led Growth: How development priorities of Bharat changed after 2014 - Organiser
articles.summary: From Subsidy Politics to Infrastructure-led Growth: How development priorities of Bharat changed after 2014  Organiser
articles.full_text:
India’s development journey over the past two decades reflects two different approaches to public spending and economic priorities. Between 2004 and 2014, under the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA), a significant share of government expenditure went towards subsidies and welfare programmes. After 2014, under the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA), infrastructure development and capital expenditure became central to the government’s economic strategy.
The difference is not that one government spent on welfare while the other abandoned it. Both governments ran welfare programmes and invested in infrastructure. The more important distinction lies in the scale and direction of public investment. The NDA government has significantly expanded capital expenditure and placed greater emphasis on creating physical and economic infrastructure that can improve connectivity, support businesses, generate employment and strengthen the country’s productive capacity.
A recent report by Swarajya, titled Modi’s Achievements In Infrastructure Creation Are Celebrated, But Its Scale Is Still Under-Appreciated, makes the broader case that the scale of infrastructure creation under Prime Minister Narendra Modi is not always fully recognised.
I was stunned to see this chart
In UPA era, India was spending all its money on subsidies and handouts
See the change after 2014!
Now India spends its money on building India: roads, railways, ports, etc…
Every Indian needs to know this pic.twitter.com/33fVYuVqhI
— Abhishek (@AbhishBanerj) October 28, 2026
The comparison raises an important question: how did India’s public spending priorities change after 2014, and what has this shift meant for the country’s economic capacity?
UPA’s subsidy-heavy approach and the fiscal challenge
The UPA government came to power in 2004 and remained in office until 2014. During this period, the Congress-led government expanded several welfare and subsidy programmes, including the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), the National Rural Health Mission and the food and fertiliser subsidy programmes.
Some of these initiatives addressed genuine needs, particularly in rural India. However, the expansion of government support also brought a substantial fiscal burden. The growing subsidy bill, rising expenditure and high fiscal deficits became important concerns during the final years of the UPA government.
Official figures presented by the Ministry of Finance in Parliament show that the Centre’s total subsidy expenditure stood at Rs 2.17 lakh crore in 2011-12. It increased to Rs 2.57 lakh crore in 2012-13 and remained high at approximately Rs 2.56 lakh crore in 2013-14.
The major components included food, fertiliser and petroleum subsidies. In 2013-14, food subsidy was estimated at Rs 92,000 crore, fertiliser subsidy at nearly Rs 68,000 crore and petroleum subsidy at Rs 85,480 crore.
The fiscal deficit also remained elevated. It stood at 5.8 per cent of GDP in 2011-12, 4.9 per cent in 2012-13 and 4.5 per cent in 2013-14.
These figures underline the fiscal pressures confronting the government when the UPA’s second term ended. A large subsidy bill, combined with other expenditure commitments, left less room for a more aggressive expansion of public capital investment.
The question is whether expenditure was being balanced with sufficient investment in long-term productive assets.
A welfare programme can provide immediate relief, but roads, railway lines, ports, power infrastructure and industrial corridors can create economic opportunities over several decades. Infrastructure also reduces the cost of transporting goods, improves access to markets and helps businesses expand beyond established urban centres.
The NDA’s shift towards capital expenditure
After taking office in 2014, the Modi government placed infrastructure development at the centre of its economic agenda. Capital expenditure was increasingly treated as an investment in India’s future productive capacity rather than simply another component of government spending.
The change is visible in the Union Budget figures. Public capital expenditure, which was around Rs 2 lakh crore in 2014-15, has increased to Rs 12.2 lakh crore in the 2026-27 Budget.
This expansion has supported investment in highways, railways, airports, ports, urban transport, power and other infrastructure sectors. It has also been accompanied by programmes designed to improve coordination between ministries and reduce delays in project planning and execution.
The PM GatiShakti National Master Plan, for instance, seeks to bring different infrastructure projects onto a common planning platform. It aims to improve coordination between roads, railways, ports, airports, waterways and logistics networks.
The broader objective is to create an integrated transport and logistics system rather than develop individual projects in isolation.
The government’s approach has also involved expanding infrastructure in smaller cities, rural areas and regions that were historically less connected to major economic centres.
National highways: A major expansion in connectivity
One of the clearest indicators of the infrastructure push is the expansion of India’s national highway network.
According to government data, the length of national highways increased from 91,287 kilometres in 2013-14 to 1,46,204 kilometres by 2025. This represents an expansion of around 60 per cent.
The pace of highway construction has also increased. From approximately 11.6 kilometres per day in 2013-14, the construction pace reached around 34 kilometres per day in 2025, according to the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.
The expansion is not limited to the addition of road kilometres. The government has also focused on expressways, economic corridors, access-controlled highways and multi-lane roads.
The length of national highways with four or more lanes has increased substantially, while high-speed corridors have expanded from a limited network in 2014 to thousands of kilometres.
Projects under Bharatmala Pariyojana have sought to improve connectivity between industrial centres, ports, border regions and major economic hubs.
Better highways have direct economic implications. They reduce travel time, improve freight movement and make it easier for manufacturers and agricultural producers to reach markets. For businesses, improved road connectivity can reduce logistics costs and improve the reliability of supply chains.
The expansion of roads also supports tourism, construction, transport services and local economic activity.
Railways: From expansion to modernisation
Indian Railways has undergone a major infrastructure expansion since 2014. The government has increased budgetary support, accelerated electrification and invested in track capacity, station redevelopment, safety systems and modern trains.
Railway electrification is among the most significant changes. More than 45,000 route kilometres of railway electrification had been completed since 2014 by 2025, according to government figures.
The expansion of electrification reduces dependence on diesel, improves operational efficiency and supports a more energy-efficient railway network.
The introduction of Vande Bharat trains has also become a visible symbol of railway modernisation. These semi-high-speed trains have expanded intercity travel options and brought modern passenger facilities to more routes.
At the same time, the government has focused on dedicated freight corridors, railway station redevelopment, improved signalling and the deployment of the indigenous Kavach train protection system on selected routes.
Railway capital expenditure has increased substantially. Budgetary support for the sector has grown from around Rs 32,000 crore in 2014-15 to Rs 2.78 lakh crore in the 2026-27 Budget.
This investment is important because railways remain central to India’s freight and passenger movement. Greater capacity can help move goods more efficiently, support industrial production and improve connectivity between states.
Airports and regional connectivity
Civil aviation is another sector where infrastructure expansion has been significant.
The number of operational airports increased from 74 in 2014 to 165 in 2026, according to government figures. The expansion has been supported by new airport projects, terminal modernisation and regional connectivity initiatives.
The UDAN scheme, launched in 2016, was designed to make air travel more accessible by connecting underserved and unserved destinations. It has helped expand air connectivity beyond major metropolitan cities.
As of 2026, the scheme had connected 95 airports, heliports and water aerodromes through 665 routes, benefiting more than 1.64 crore passengers, according to the government.
The growth of airports and regional routes has implications beyond passenger travel. It can support tourism, trade, business travel, medical access and the movement of high-value goods.
For smaller cities, improved air connectivity can also make them more attractive destinations for investment.
Metro networks and urban infrastructure
Urban transport has emerged as another major area of investment. India’s metro network has expanded from around 248 kilometres in five cities in 2014 to more than 1,155 kilometres in 2026.
The number of cities with metro connectivity has also increased significantly. Metro projects are now operational in several cities beyond Delhi, Bengaluru, Kolkata and other early adopters.
The expansion of urban transport infrastructure is important as India’s cities continue to grow. Efficient public transport can reduce dependence on private vehicles, improve mobility and support the development of new residential and commercial areas.
The investment in metro rail, regional rapid transit systems and urban infrastructure reflects a broader attempt to address the demands of a rapidly urbanising economy.

articles.title: East Africa leads continental trade revival as infrastructure, regional integration gain pace - weekendargus.co.za
articles.summary: East Africa leads continental trade revival as infrastructure, regional integration gain pace  weekendargus.co.za
articles.full_text:
East Africa has emerged as the continent’s strongest-performing trade hub, buoyed by sweeping infrastructure upgrades, policy coordination and rising business confidence, according to the latest Africa Trade Barometer (ATB) released by Standard Bank Group.
The fifth edition of the survey, which covers 10 major African markets and released on Thursday, found that firms are reporting improvements across all major infrastructure categories for the first time since the barometer’s launch in 2022.
The report includes Angola, Ghana, Kenya, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia. Together these markets account for about 68% of Sub-Saharan Africa’s GDP, making the findings a significant indicator of broader continental trade trends.
South Africa dropped from 1st to 2nd place, while Namibia fell to 3rd, Kenya to 7th, and Zambia to 10th. Nigeria, Tanzania, and Uganda remained stable, retaining their positions at 5th, 4th, and 9th, respectively.
Philip Myburgh, head of trade for business and commercial banking at Standard Bank Group, said the improvements signal growing investment in logistics capacity and digital trade systems.
“Across the 10 markets we surveyed, firms reported improvements across every major infrastructure category, including power, telecommunications, road, rail, ports and digital border systems,” Myburgh said.
“This marks the first time since the Africa Trade Barometer’s launch that all infrastructure indicators have improved simultaneously, reflecting growing investment in logistics capacity and digital trade facilitation across the continent.”
Growth is projected to reach around 4.3% in 2026, supported by moderating inflation in seven of the 10 economies and improvements in external debt positions.
The barometer’s business confidence index rose to 65, with most firms expecting stronger turnover and more stable trading conditions. Strong demand and prices for commodities such as gold, platinum and copper have provided a boost to exporters and foreign exchange earnings across several economies.
Regional trade integration is also gathering momentum. Awareness of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) has reached 50% among surveyed firms, with businesses increasingly recognising its potential to ease the movement of goods, expand market access and support industrialisation.
The report noted that early AfCFTA-enabled shipments are already demonstrating practical progress in facilitating cross-border trade.
East Africa emerged as the strongest-performing sub-region in the latest survey, recording a 10-percentage-point increase in export activity. The report attributes this growth to policy coordination and trade facilitation reforms across the region.
Kenya is playing a central role in strengthening regional integration. A recent Kenya–Uganda trade reclassification, which treats goods originating in Kenya as intra-regional transfers rather than imports, has reduced administrative friction within the East African Community.
At the same time, Kenya and Tanzania have renewed commitments to remove non-tariff barriers that had previously slowed cross-border trade. These reforms are being supported by major upgrades to the Northern and Central transport corridors, which are improving logistics efficiency by reducing border delays and strengthening supply-chain reliability.
For businesses operating in the region, the improvements are translating into lower transaction costs and greater confidence in expanding cross-border operations.
The report also highlighted changes in global trade relationships.
It said recent tariff shifts affecting access to the United States have contributed to declining engagement with US trade partners among surveyed firms. At the same time, businesses are increasingly turning to Asian markets, particularly China, as key sourcing partners.
Companies cited competitive pricing, broader product variety, faster response times and stronger supply-chain reliability as reasons for growing trade with Asian suppliers.
Digital payment systems are also transforming cross-border trade across the continent.
The survey found that 78% of cross-border sales and 79% of purchases are now facilitated through digital payments, supported by bank-led platforms, mobile-money integration and the expansion of the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS).
PAPSS allows businesses to settle transactions in local currencies, reducing reliance on hard currencies and speeding up cross-border payments.
Despite the positive trends, climate-related pressures remain a concern for businesses. About 38% of firms reported shifts in demand linked to climate impacts, while 32% cited productivity losses, highlighting the need for more resilient infrastructure and production systems.
The report concluded that Africa’s trade outlook is improving as infrastructure investment, macroeconomic stabilisation and regional integration gather pace. However, geopolitical risks — including ongoing tensions in the Middle East — could introduce volatility in energy prices and supply chains, potentially affecting trade costs in the near term.
Myburgh said continued progress on AfCFTA implementation would be critical in sustaining the positive momentum.
“As AfCFTA implementation deepens, and as more countries harmonise customs, regulatory frameworks and logistics platforms, Africa’s ability to expand industrial capacity, scale regional value chains and strengthen competitiveness is set to accelerate,” he said.
